groups.name: Input and accessibility
groups.note: Use this group to reason about operability, assistive technology behavior, focus/input semantics, and whether UI changes are perceivable to more than just a visual mouse user.

topics.title: Pointer events
topics.summary: Pointer events unify mouse, touch, pen, and stylus input behind one event model. A strong explanation covers pointerId, pointerType, pressure, pointer capture, cancellation, and why duplicating mouse/touch logic creates gesture bugs.

topics.title: ARIA live regions internals
topics.summary: ARIA live regions are parts of the DOM that assistive technologies monitor for announcements. The important details are politeness level, atomic updates, insertion timing, and avoiding rapid DOM replacement that screen readers may ignore.

topics.title: Accessibility tree
topics.summary: The accessibility tree is the browser-derived semantic representation exposed to assistive technologies. It is built from DOM, native semantics, ARIA, CSS visibility, names, descriptions, focusability, and platform mappings.

groups.name: Rendering correctness and state
groups.note: Use this group to make UI behavior repeatable under retries, concurrency, async races, and partial failure.

topics.title: Idempotent UI actions
topics.summary: An idempotent UI action produces the same durable result even if the user clicks twice, the request retries, or the component remounts. The usual tools are action keys, disabled states, dedupe maps, idempotency headers, and server-side replay protection.

topics.title: Deterministic rendering
topics.summary: Deterministic rendering means the same inputs produce the same UI output. It avoids hidden time, random values, mutable globals, request order dependence, and client/server mismatches during hydration.

topics.title: Priority inversion in async code
topics.summary: Priority inversion happens when urgent work waits behind lower-priority work because the scheduler or promise chain cannot preempt it. In UI this shows up as input blocked behind rendering, background fetches, or heavy microtask chains.

topics.title: Race conditions in UI state
topics.summary: UI state races happen when async results arrive out of order or after the state they depended on has changed. Common fixes are request IDs, AbortController, version checks, state machines, and idempotent reducers.

groups.name: Performance and Web Vitals
groups.note: Use this group to connect browser metrics to concrete causes: network, parsing, main-thread work, layout, paint, and input latency.

topics.title: Speculative prerendering
topics.summary: Speculative prerendering asks the browser to prepare likely future navigations before the user clicks. It can make navigations instant, but must avoid private-state leaks, side effects, wasted bandwidth, and analytics double-counting.

topics.title: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
topics.summary: LCP measures when the largest visible content element in the viewport is rendered. Good explanations connect LCP to TTFB, render-blocking CSS, image discovery, resource priority, server rendering, and client-side render delays.

topics.title: Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
topics.summary: CLS measures unexpected visual movement during page lifetime. The core prevention model is reserving space, stable dimensions, predictable font loading, non-intrusive ads/embeds, and avoiding DOM insertions above existing content.

topics.title: Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
topics.summary: INP measures the latency of user interactions from input through processing to the next paint. It rewards short event handlers, quick style/layout work, cooperative yielding, and avoiding long main-thread tasks.

topics.title: First Input Delay (FID)
topics.summary: FID measured the delay before the browser could start processing the first input. It is largely a main-thread availability metric and is best explained historically as the predecessor to INP for interaction responsiveness.

topics.title: Long tasks API
topics.summary: The Long Tasks API exposes main-thread tasks that run long enough to block input and rendering. It is useful for finding expensive scripts, hydration bursts, synchronous parsing, and third-party code that creates responsiveness cliffs.

topics.title: PerformanceObserver API
topics.summary: PerformanceObserver streams browser or runtime performance entries as they occur, often with buffered historical entries. It is the common mechanism for collecting vitals, resource timing, long tasks, marks, and measures.

groups.name: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
groups.note: Use this group to reason about resource lifetime, browser memory retention, stream flow control, workers, transfer, and media/data channels.

topics.title: Garbage collection timing
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Garbage collection is nondeterministic and should not be part of application correctness. A frontend engineer should understand object reachability, closures, event listeners, WeakMap/WeakRef trade-offs, and why GC pauses can affect responsiveness.

topics.title: Detached DOM nodes
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Detached DOM nodes are removed from the visible document but still retained by JavaScript references. They often come from leaked listeners, caches, closures, observers, and component cleanup bugs.

topics.title: Browser memory leak detection
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Browser memory leak detection is the process of proving memory grows because objects remain reachable after expected cleanup. Good explanations include heap snapshots, allocation timelines, detached DOM node views, listener cleanup, and reproducible interaction loops.

topics.title: Streaming fetch response handling
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Streaming fetch handling reads response chunks as they arrive instead of waiting for the full body. It enables progressive rendering, lower memory usage, server-sent protocols, and earlier cancellation.

topics.title: AbortController
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: AbortController coordinates cancellation for fetches, streams, event listeners, and async operations. It prevents stale updates, leaked work, unnecessary network traffic, and component-unmount races.

topics.title: Backpressure in streams API
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Backpressure is the signal that a consumer cannot keep up with a producer. Streams expose it through desiredSize, writer.ready, highWaterMark, drain-like behavior, and async pulls to avoid unbounded buffering.

topics.title: WebRTC
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: WebRTC provides peer-to-peer media and data channels with NAT traversal, ICE, STUN/TURN, SDP negotiation, encryption, congestion control, and real-time delivery constraints.

topics.title: IndexedDB
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: IndexedDB is the browser's transactional object store for larger structured data. Good explanations mention version upgrades, object stores, indexes, transactions, async request APIs, quota, and offline-first storage.

topics.title: WebAssembly integration
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: WebAssembly integration loads compiled modules into JavaScript for CPU-heavy, portable code. The real boundary is memory copying, async instantiation, imports/exports, streaming compilation, and choosing where JS remains simpler.

topics.title: OffscreenCanvas
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: OffscreenCanvas allows canvas rendering off the main thread, often in a Worker. It is useful for charts, games, image processing, and avoiding main-thread paint pressure.

topics.title: Transferable objects
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Transferable objects move ownership of buffers or ports between threads without copying. After transfer, the original owner is detached, which improves performance but requires explicit lifetime handling.

topics.title: SharedArrayBuffer
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: SharedArrayBuffer allows multiple threads to access the same memory with Atomics for coordination. In browsers it requires cross-origin isolation because of side-channel risk.

topics.title: Web Workers vs Service Workers
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Web Workers run background JavaScript for a page; Service Workers act as network/proxy lifecycle scripts for an origin scope. Workers help CPU isolation, while Service Workers intercept requests, cache, and enable offline behavior.

topics.title: Web Components interoperability
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Web Components interoperate through custom elements, attributes, properties, events, slots, and DOM APIs. Good boundaries avoid framework-specific assumptions and expose stable platform contracts.

topics.title: Custom Elements lifecycle
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Custom Elements lifecycle callbacks handle construction, connection, disconnection, adoption, and observed attribute changes. Correct components defer DOM work until connected and clean up listeners, observers, and async work on disconnect.

topics.title: Shadow DOM
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Shadow DOM creates an encapsulated DOM subtree with scoped styling and slot-based composition. It improves component isolation but affects styling, event retargeting, accessibility names, and testing strategies.

groups.name: Offline, collaboration, and data modeling
groups.note: Use this group to model state transitions, conflicts, merges, rollback, and event histories explicitly instead of treating the frontend as throwaway state.

topics.title: CRDT basics for collaboration
topics.summary: CRDTs are data types designed so replicas can update independently and merge without conflicts. A clear answer covers commutativity, associativity, idempotent merges, causal metadata, and trade-offs in metadata size.

topics.title: Offline conflict resolution
topics.summary: Offline conflict resolution decides what happens when local changes meet remote changes after reconnect. Strategies include last-write-wins, field-level merge, operational transforms, CRDTs, manual conflict UI, and version vectors.

topics.title: Optimistic UI rollback strategy
topics.summary: Optimistic UI applies a predicted result immediately, then confirms or rolls back after the server responds. A reliable strategy records previous state, pending operation IDs, failure rules, and reconciliation with server truth.

topics.title: Event sourcing in frontend
topics.summary: Frontend event sourcing stores user/domain events and derives UI state from projections. It helps with undo/redo, offline queues, auditability, replay, optimistic updates, and deterministic debugging.

topics.title: Finite state modeling
topics.summary: Finite state modeling describes UI behavior as explicit states and allowed transitions. It prevents impossible states like loading and saved simultaneously, and makes retries, errors, and cancellation easier to test.

groups.name: Frontend architecture and rendering models
groups.note: Use this group to compare client rendering, server rendering, islands, hydration, server components, micro-frontends, and concurrent rendering trade-offs.

topics.title: Micro-frontend orchestration
topics.summary: Micro-frontend orchestration coordinates independently built frontend applications at runtime. Strong explanations cover ownership boundaries, routing, shared dependencies, CSS isolation, versioning, event contracts, and failure containment.

topics.title: Edge rendering
topics.summary: Edge rendering produces HTML or responses close to users, usually in geographically distributed runtimes. It improves latency but constrains APIs, cold starts, data locality, cache behavior, and consistency.

topics.title: Server components
topics.summary: Server components render parts of the component tree on the server without shipping their implementation to the client. The core trade-off is reduced client JavaScript versus stricter serialization, data access, and boundary rules.

topics.title: Selective hydration
topics.summary: Selective hydration hydrates only the interactive parts of server-rendered HTML, often by priority or visibility. It reduces startup work, but requires accurate island boundaries and safe event replay or delayed interactivity.

topics.title: Suspense boundaries
topics.summary: Suspense boundaries isolate async waiting so one slow dependency does not block the entire UI. A strong explanation mentions fallback UI, reveal order, thrown promises/resource reads, streaming SSR, and avoiding waterfalls.

topics.title: Render waterfalls
topics.summary: Render waterfalls happen when rendering discovers async dependencies sequentially instead of in parallel. They commonly occur in nested components, route loaders, dynamic imports, and suspense trees that fetch too late.

topics.title: Scheduler priorities
topics.summary: Scheduler priorities decide which work should run now and which work can wait. UI schedulers prioritize input and visible updates over background rendering, prefetching, analytics, and non-urgent transitions.

topics.title: Tearing in concurrent UI
topics.summary: Tearing occurs when different parts of the UI observe different versions of shared state during concurrent rendering. Avoid it with consistent snapshots, subscription protocols, immutable commits, and framework-specific external-store APIs.

topics.title: Streaming SSR
topics.summary: Streaming SSR sends HTML progressively while data or components are still resolving. It improves time to first byte and progressive display, but requires boundary management, script ordering, and hydration coordination.

topics.title: Islands architecture
topics.summary: Islands architecture renders mostly static HTML and hydrates isolated interactive components. It reduces client JavaScript and hydration cost, but boundaries and cross-island communication must be explicit.

topics.title: Partial hydration
topics.summary: Partial hydration hydrates only parts of a server-rendered page rather than the full tree. It is related to islands and resumability, and trades framework complexity for less startup JavaScript.

topics.title: Hydration
topics.summary: Hydration attaches client behavior to server-rendered HTML. The hard parts are matching server/client output, event replay, async data consistency, and avoiding large startup work.

groups.name: Security, networking, and caching
groups.note: Use this group to explain browser security boundaries, request policies, cache semantics, and delivery hints.

topics.title: Prototype pollution
topics.summary: Prototype pollution lets attacker-controlled keys modify Object.prototype or constructors. It often comes from unsafe deep merge, path setters, query parsers, or JSON merge logic that accepts __proto__, prototype, or constructor keys.

topics.title: DOM clobbering
topics.summary: DOM clobbering abuses named elements or IDs that become properties on document, forms, or windows. Safe code avoids trusting global property lookup and reads explicit attributes from selected elements instead.

topics.title: Trusted Types
topics.summary: Trusted Types is a browser defense that restricts dangerous DOM sinks such as innerHTML to values created by approved policies. It is especially useful for reducing DOM XSS in large applications.

topics.title: Content Security Policy (CSP)
topics.summary: CSP is a browser-enforced policy controlling where scripts, styles, images, frames, and other resources can load from. Strong explanations cover nonces, hashes, strict-dynamic, report-only rollout, and blocking inline script execution.

topics.title: CSRF vs XSS mitigation
topics.summary: CSRF tricks an authenticated browser into sending unwanted state-changing requests; XSS executes attacker script in the trusted origin. CSRF is mitigated with SameSite, tokens, and origin checks; XSS is mitigated with output encoding, CSP, sanitization, and Trusted Types.

topics.title: SameSite cookie modes
topics.summary: SameSite controls whether cookies are sent on cross-site requests. Lax is a pragmatic default, Strict is more protective but can break flows, and None requires Secure for third-party contexts.

topics.title: CORS preflight
topics.summary: A CORS preflight is an OPTIONS request the browser sends before non-simple cross-origin requests. The server must explicitly allow origin, methods, and headers; CORS is a browser boundary, not server-to-server auth.

topics.title: Preload vs Prefetch vs Preconnect
topics.summary: Preload fetches a needed resource for the current navigation, prefetch gets likely future resources at lower priority, and preconnect warms DNS/TCP/TLS connections to an origin. Misuse can waste bandwidth or hurt priority scheduling.

topics.title: Priority hints
topics.summary: Priority hints communicate relative fetch importance to the browser. They are useful for hero images and noncritical assets, but should complement rather than replace correct resource discovery and markup order.

topics.title: HTTP/3 and QUIC
topics.summary: HTTP/3 runs HTTP semantics over QUIC instead of TCP. It reduces transport head-of-line blocking, integrates TLS 1.3, supports connection migration, and handles loss recovery per stream more gracefully than HTTP/2 over TCP.

topics.title: ETag vs Cache-Control
topics.summary: Cache-Control defines freshness and reuse rules; ETag is a validator for conditional revalidation. Effective caching uses both: freshness for fast reuse and validators for cheap correctness after stale entries.

topics.title: Stale-while-revalidate
topics.summary: Stale-while-revalidate serves a cached stale response immediately while refreshing in the background. It improves perceived latency but requires tolerance for temporary staleness and careful invalidation for user-specific data.

topics.title: Cache invalidation strategies
topics.summary: Cache invalidation is the policy for removing or superseding cached data when truth changes. Techniques include TTLs, versioned keys, surrogate keys, write-through updates, event-driven purges, and scoped cache busting.

topics.title: Service Worker lifecycle traps
topics.summary: Service Workers have install, waiting, activate, fetch, and update states that can keep old code alive. Traps include stale caches, uncontrolled clients, skipWaiting misuse, update races, and broken offline fallbacks.

groups.name: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
groups.note: Use this group to reason about browser pipeline phases, observer callbacks, compositing, containment, and avoiding accidental layout cost.

topics.title: MutationObserver cost
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: MutationObserver batches DOM mutation records, but broad subtree observation can be expensive. The cost comes from record volume, callback work, retained nodes, and accidental feedback loops that create more mutations.

topics.title: ResizeObserver loop limits
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: ResizeObserver reports element size changes, but writing size-affecting styles inside the callback can create loops. Browsers limit these loops, so callbacks should defer writes and avoid recursive layout changes.

topics.title: IntersectionObserver internals
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: IntersectionObserver asynchronously reports visibility intersections between targets and a root. It avoids many scroll-handler costs, but callbacks are still approximate, threshold-based, and affected by root margins and layout changes.

topics.title: Subpixel rendering
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: Subpixel rendering occurs because layout uses fractional CSS pixels while screens use device pixels. Rounding can affect text, transforms, borders, canvas drawing, and alignment across devicePixelRatio values.

topics.title: CSS containment
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: CSS containment tells the browser that layout, paint, style, or size effects are isolated. It lets the engine skip broader invalidation and is especially useful for virtualized lists, cards, and independent widgets.

topics.title: GPU acceleration in CSS
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: GPU acceleration usually means moving compositable work such as transforms and opacity to compositor layers. It can improve animation smoothness but too many layers waste memory and can hurt performance.

topics.title: Paint vs composite vs layout
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: Layout computes geometry, paint rasterizes pixels, and composite assembles layers on screen. Performance work often means avoiding layout and paint when a transform or opacity-only composite will do.

topics.title: Browser compositing layers
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: Compositing layers are independently rasterized surfaces the compositor can move or blend. They are created by transforms, opacity, video, fixed elements, will-change, and browser heuristics, but each layer has memory and upload cost.

topics.title: Layout thrashing
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: Layout thrashing alternates DOM reads that force layout with writes that invalidate layout. Batch reads before writes, use transforms for motion, and avoid measuring after each mutation.

groups.name: Bundling, modules, and delivery
groups.note: Use this group to explain how JavaScript reaches the browser, how chunks are split, and what makes code removable or render-blocking.

topics.title: Module federation
topics.summary: Module federation loads code from independently deployed builds at runtime. It enables separate ownership and deployment but introduces version negotiation, shared dependency, fallback, security, and observability problems.

topics.title: Dynamic import chunking
topics.summary: Dynamic import creates async module boundaries that bundlers can split into separate chunks. It is useful for route-level, feature-level, and conditionally loaded code, but too many chunks create network overhead.

topics.title: Code splitting strategies
topics.summary: Code splitting decides which code ships together and which code loads later. Useful strategies include route splitting, component splitting, vendor splitting, permission-based loading, and interaction-triggered loading.

topics.title: Tree shaking internals
topics.summary: Tree shaking removes unused exports by static analysis of ESM imports/exports. It works best with side-effect-free modules, direct imports, and package sideEffects metadata.

topics.title: Render blocking resources
topics.summary: Render-blocking resources delay first paint or meaningful rendering because the browser must fetch, parse, or execute them first. CSS, synchronous scripts, fonts, and late-discovered hero assets are common causes.

topics.title: Critical rendering path
topics.summary: The critical rendering path is the sequence from HTML bytes to DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, and composite. Optimizing it means reducing blocking resources and making important content discoverable early.

groups.name: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
groups.note: Use this group to reason about scheduling, stale closures, identity, structural sharing, diffing, reconciliation, and cooperative rendering.

topics.title: Task starvation
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Task starvation happens when one class of work keeps the event loop from processing another. Infinite microtask chains, heavy sync loops, or too many high-priority tasks can starve input, timers, rendering, or I/O.

topics.title: Event loop (macro vs microtasks)
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: The event loop runs synchronous code, then microtasks, then macrotasks and rendering opportunities. Promises and queueMicrotask run before timers, which can be good for consistency but dangerous when chains are unbounded.

topics.title: Stale closure problem
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: A stale closure uses values captured from an earlier render or state version. It appears in handlers, timers, promises, subscriptions, and memoized callbacks that outlive the data they closed over.

topics.title: Memoization pitfalls
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Memoization can hide expensive work, but wrong keys, mutable inputs, unbounded caches, and referential churn can make it incorrect or slower. It is a trade-off between CPU, memory, invalidation, and complexity.

topics.title: Referential equality
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Referential equality compares object identity rather than deep value. UI frameworks use it for memoization and update detection, so recreating objects or functions can trigger unnecessary work.

topics.title: Immutable data patterns
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Immutable data patterns create new values instead of mutating existing state. They make change detection, undo, time travel, concurrency, and structural sharing easier.

topics.title: Structural sharing
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Structural sharing reuses unchanged parts of immutable data structures. It reduces memory churn and lets referential equality identify which subtrees changed.

topics.title: Virtual DOM diffing complexity
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Virtual DOM diffing compares previous and next trees to compute DOM operations. Keys reduce expensive ambiguity in lists, while unstable keys or deep tree churn increase work and bugs.

topics.title: Fiber architecture
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Fiber architecture breaks rendering work into interruptible units. It enables prioritization, pausing, resuming, aborting, and committing work separately from rendering calculations.

topics.title: Reconciliation algorithm
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Reconciliation decides how a framework maps a new UI description onto existing component or DOM instances. Keyed identity, component type, position, and state preservation rules are central.

topics.title: Time slicing
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Time slicing breaks long rendering or computation into chunks so the event loop can process input and paint. It improves responsiveness but requires work to be restartable and side effects to be delayed.

topics.title: Concurrent rendering
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Concurrent rendering lets a framework prepare new UI without immediately committing it. It enables interruptible rendering and prioritization, but requires avoiding side effects during render and preventing tearing.

groups.name: Code structure and modularity
groups.note: Use this group to reason about module shape, dependency direction, abstraction, information hiding, and how local code structure affects future change.

topics.title: Cohesion and coupling
topics.summary: Cohesion measures how strongly the responsibilities inside a module belong together, while coupling measures how much that module depends on other modules. Good software engineering raises cohesion and controls coupling so changes stay local.

topics.title: Abstraction boundaries
topics.summary: An abstraction boundary exposes what callers need while hiding volatile implementation details. The boundary should make correct use easier, make invalid use harder, and leave room for implementation changes.

topics.title: Information hiding
topics.summary: Information hiding keeps decisions that are likely to change inside one module instead of leaking them into every caller. It protects code from ripple effects when storage, parsing, algorithms, or vendor behavior changes.

topics.title: Dependency direction
topics.summary: Dependency direction decides which modules know about which other modules. Stable business rules should not depend on volatile delivery details such as HTTP, CLIs, files, framework adapters, or UI shells.

topics.title: Composition over inheritance
topics.summary: Composition builds behavior by passing collaborators or functions together, while inheritance shares behavior through parent classes. Composition usually makes behavior easier to test, replace, and combine without deep class hierarchies.

groups.name: Modeling, APIs, and contracts
groups.note: Use this group to express business rules, invariants, outcomes, and compatibility expectations directly in code boundaries.

topics.title: Domain modeling
topics.summary: Domain modeling captures the names, rules, states, and workflows of the problem space in code. Strong models reduce translation errors between product language, data structures, and business behavior.

topics.title: Invariants
topics.summary: Invariants are facts that must remain true before and after operations. Naming invariants explicitly turns hidden assumptions into validations, tests, constructors, and state transition rules.

topics.title: Value objects
topics.summary: Value objects represent values by their contents instead of identity. They are useful for money, email addresses, quantities, ranges, and other concepts that need validation and equality semantics.

topics.title: Error handling strategy
topics.summary: Error handling strategy decides which failures throw, which return typed outcomes, which retry, which are user-visible, and which are programmer bugs. A consistent strategy keeps failures inspectable instead of accidental.

topics.title: Result types and explicit outcomes
topics.summary: Result types represent success and failure as data. They are useful when callers are expected to branch on known outcomes such as validation failures, missing records, authorization decisions, or conflicts.

topics.title: API contracts inside a codebase
topics.summary: Internal APIs still need contracts: inputs, outputs, side effects, errors, ordering, idempotency, and compatibility expectations. Clear internal contracts reduce coordination cost between modules and teams.

topics.title: Backward-compatible change
topics.summary: Backward-compatible change lets existing callers continue working while new behavior rolls out. Practical compatibility includes additive fields, tolerant readers, deprecation windows, feature flags, and migration helpers.

groups.name: Testing and quality signals
groups.note: Use this group to choose tests that prove useful behavior instead of only executing implementation details.

topics.title: Unit test boundaries
topics.summary: Unit tests should focus on meaningful behavior at a stable boundary, not private implementation trivia. Good unit boundaries make fast tests valuable while leaving room to refactor internals.

topics.title: Integration test boundaries
topics.summary: Integration tests verify that real collaborators work together across module, process, storage, or protocol boundaries. They should cover risky contracts that unit tests cannot prove.

topics.title: Test doubles
topics.summary: Test doubles replace real collaborators with fakes, stubs, spies, or mocks. They are useful when the double preserves the contract being tested, but harmful when they only mirror implementation details.

topics.title: Property-based testing
topics.summary: Property-based testing checks general rules across many generated inputs instead of only named examples. It is useful for parsers, formatters, reducers, validators, and algorithms with durable invariants.

topics.title: Mutation testing
topics.summary: Mutation testing changes code in small ways and checks whether tests fail. Surviving mutations show where tests execute code without proving the behavior that matters.

groups.name: Refactoring and evolution
groups.note: Use this group to change code safely over time while managing debt, legacy behavior, toggles, and maintainability signals.

topics.title: Refactoring in small steps
topics.summary: Refactoring changes code structure without changing observable behavior. Small verified steps reduce risk by keeping each move understandable, reversible, and covered by existing or characterization tests.

topics.title: Code smells
topics.summary: Code smells are signals that code may be harder to change than necessary. Long functions, shotgun changes, primitive obsession, feature envy, and duplicate logic are prompts to investigate, not automatic verdicts.

topics.title: Technical debt management
topics.summary: Technical debt is a design or implementation trade-off that creates future carrying cost. Good debt management names the cost, owner, trigger for repayment, and risk if it remains unpaid.

topics.title: Legacy code characterization
topics.summary: Characterization tests capture what legacy code currently does before changing it. They create a safety net when requirements are unclear, behavior is surprising, or refactoring must preserve quirks.

topics.title: Feature toggle cleanup
topics.summary: Feature toggles should have owners, expiry dates, and cleanup plans. Stale toggles create hidden branches, test matrix growth, configuration risk, and dead code.

groups.name: Collaboration and delivery discipline
groups.note: Use this group to make software work reviewable, explainable, sliceable, and maintainable across a team.

topics.title: Code review quality
topics.summary: Code review quality depends on reviewing behavior, risk, maintainability, tests, naming, compatibility, and operational impact. Reviews should make the change better without becoming a style-only gate.

topics.title: Architecture decision records
topics.summary: Architecture decision records capture the context, options, decision, and consequences of important technical choices. They help future engineers understand why a design exists before changing it.

topics.title: Estimation and risk slicing
topics.summary: Estimation improves when work is sliced around uncertainty, dependencies, feedback, and irreversible decisions. Risk-first slices turn unknowns into evidence before committing to a large implementation path.

topics.title: Documentation close to code
topics.summary: Documentation close to code keeps examples, contracts, commands, and design notes near the implementation they describe. It reduces drift when docs can be reviewed and regenerated with code changes.

groups.name: Debugging, configuration, and runtime behavior
groups.note: Use this group to connect everyday code decisions to diagnosis, configuration safety, logs, profiling, and production behavior.

topics.title: Systematic debugging
topics.summary: Systematic debugging forms a hypothesis, chooses the smallest useful observation, compares expected and actual behavior, and updates the model. It prevents random edits from hiding the real cause.

topics.title: Contextual logging
topics.summary: Contextual logging records enough stable identifiers and state to reconstruct behavior without dumping sensitive data. Good logs explain what happened, where, for whom, and why the code chose that path.

topics.title: Configuration boundaries
topics.summary: Configuration boundaries separate code from environment-specific values while keeping validation close to startup. Strong config boundaries prevent missing, misspelled, or incompatible settings from failing deep in runtime.

topics.title: Performance profiling before optimization
topics.summary: Performance profiling measures where time, memory, or I/O is actually spent before changing code. Profiling protects teams from optimizing the wrong path or trading clarity for unmeasured speed.

groups.name: Foundations and taxonomy
groups.note: Use this group to clarify what the design system owns, how design and engineering collaborate, and how shared UI language stays coherent across products.

topics.title: Design system purpose and governance
topics.summary: A design system is the operating layer between product design, UI engineering, and shipped interfaces. Governance defines who can change tokens, components, Figma libraries, package APIs, documentation, and release policy.

topics.title: Component inventory and audit
topics.summary: A component inventory identifies repeated UI patterns, implementation variants, usage frequency, accessibility risk, and ownership gaps. It turns vague design debt into a prioritized system backlog.

topics.title: Design language taxonomy
topics.summary: Design language taxonomy names the primitives, patterns, templates, and product-specific exceptions in a shared vocabulary. Clear taxonomy keeps Figma names, component names, token names, and documentation aligned.

topics.title: Accessibility as a design constraint
topics.summary: Accessibility belongs in design decisions before implementation. Color contrast, focus order, target size, motion, labels, keyboard behavior, and error messaging should be treated as design constraints, not late QA fixes.

topics.title: Contribution model and ownership
topics.summary: A contribution model explains how teams propose, review, build, document, and release system changes. It defines ownership across design, engineering, accessibility, product, and platform maintainers.

groups.name: Tokens and theming
groups.note: Use this group to connect Figma variables, semantic tokens, code outputs, themes, and migration paths without letting visual decisions drift between tools.

topics.title: Design token architecture
topics.summary: Design token architecture separates raw values, semantic decisions, component aliases, and platform outputs. This lets a color, spacing, typography, or motion decision move from design source to code without hardcoded drift.

topics.title: Token naming and semantic layers
topics.summary: Token names should encode intent rather than current visual appearance. Semantic layers such as surface, text, border, action, and feedback survive rebrands better than names like blue-500 or gray-light.

topics.title: Figma variables to code tokens
topics.summary: Figma variables become reliable code tokens only when naming, modes, aliases, exports, review, and versioning are explicit. The pipeline should detect missing mappings before app code consumes broken values.

topics.title: Theme modes and brand theming
topics.summary: Theme modes map the same semantic token names to different values for light, dark, high-contrast, brand, or tenant contexts. The component API should consume stable semantics, not mode-specific literals.

topics.title: Token versioning and migration
topics.summary: Token versioning protects consuming apps when a token is renamed, removed, or changes meaning. Migration notes, aliases, deprecation windows, and codemods keep design changes from becoming scattered UI regressions.

groups.name: Figma and design-code handoff
groups.note: Use this group to make design intent inspectable and traceable through variants, responsive constraints, specs, issues, and acceptance criteria.

topics.title: Figma component variants
topics.summary: Figma variants model the supported visual states and options for a component. They should map closely to code props so designers and engineers are discussing the same combinations and constraints.

topics.title: Auto layout and responsive constraints
topics.summary: Auto layout and responsive constraints make design intent explicit for spacing, wrapping, alignment, truncation, and resizing. They reduce ambiguity when a Figma frame becomes real CSS layout.

topics.title: Design spec handoff quality
topics.summary: Design handoff quality depends on states, content rules, accessibility notes, responsive behavior, data edge cases, and interaction timing. A polished static frame is not enough to implement durable UI.

topics.title: GitHub issues for design changes
topics.summary: GitHub issues connect design requests to engineering review, implementation, tests, release notes, and linked Figma evidence. They make design system changes traceable instead of scattered across comments and chat.

topics.title: Design review acceptance criteria
topics.summary: Design review acceptance criteria define what must be true before a component change ships: visual match, accessible behavior, documented states, responsive behavior, analytics impact, and migration guidance.

groups.name: Component API and implementation
groups.note: Use this group to translate design decisions into stable component APIs, composition models, state contracts, and styling rules.

topics.title: Component prop API design
topics.summary: Component prop APIs translate design intent into reusable engineering interfaces. Good APIs expose stable semantic choices, prevent invalid combinations, and leave room for content and accessibility requirements.

topics.title: Slots composition and escape hatches
topics.summary: Slots and composition let product teams place custom content inside system components without forking them. Escape hatches should be deliberate, documented, and constrained so they do not undermine consistency.

topics.title: Controlled vs uncontrolled components
topics.summary: Controlled components let app state own the value, while uncontrolled components keep internal state until a boundary event. Design system components should choose the model that matches validation, form, and composition needs.

topics.title: Visual states and interaction contracts
topics.summary: Visual states such as hover, focus, disabled, loading, selected, invalid, and pressed are interaction contracts. They should be represented in design, documentation, tests, and implementation with the same names.

topics.title: Styling strategy for component libraries
topics.summary: A component library styling strategy decides how tokens, CSS variables, cascade layers, class names, composition, and app overrides interact. The strategy should protect consistency while allowing product-specific layout.

groups.name: Documentation, testing, and release
groups.note: Use this group to keep component behavior documented, tested, versioned, and safe for consuming teams to upgrade.

topics.title: Storybook-driven documentation
topics.summary: Storybook-style documentation pairs component examples with props, states, accessibility notes, tokens, and usage guidance. It becomes a shared review surface for design, engineering, QA, and product teams.

topics.title: Visual regression testing
topics.summary: Visual regression testing compares rendered component states across changes to catch unintended appearance shifts. It is most useful when snapshots represent real supported states instead of random page screenshots.

topics.title: Interaction and accessibility tests
topics.summary: Interaction and accessibility tests verify keyboard flow, focus management, ARIA state, labels, disabled behavior, and event timing. They protect behavior that visual review alone cannot reliably catch.

topics.title: Changelog and release notes for components
topics.summary: Component changelogs explain what changed, why it changed, what apps must update, and whether visual or behavioral snapshots should be reviewed. They make design system releases consumable by product teams.

topics.title: Deprecation and migration playbooks
topics.summary: Deprecation playbooks give teams a path away from old tokens, props, variants, or components. Good migrations include timelines, warnings, codemods, examples, support windows, and removal criteria.

groups.name: Adoption and operations
groups.note: Use this group to treat the design system as a product with roadmap, coverage, governance, package distribution, and debt management.

topics.title: Adoption metrics and coverage
topics.summary: Adoption metrics show where the design system is used, bypassed, forked, or missing. Coverage data helps prioritize components, migrations, docs, and support work based on real product impact.

topics.title: Cross-team design system roadmap
topics.summary: A cross-team roadmap balances product needs, accessibility fixes, token migrations, component quality, design language evolution, and platform investment. It keeps the system from becoming only a component backlog.

topics.title: Design debt triage
topics.summary: Design debt triage ranks inconsistent UI, missing states, token drift, inaccessible patterns, and local component forks by user impact and implementation cost. It turns inconsistency into managed product debt.

topics.title: Governance between Figma and GitHub
topics.summary: Figma and GitHub governance defines how design decisions become reviewed code changes, packages, docs, and releases. The goal is traceable alignment between the design source of truth and shipped UI components.

topics.title: Package distribution and consuming apps
topics.summary: Design system packages must work for consuming apps with clear peer dependencies, build outputs, versioning, tree shaking, CSS loading, and upgrade guidance. Distribution quality determines whether teams can adopt the system safely.

groups.name: Transport and protocol internals
groups.note: Use this group to reason about how bytes move over the network, what happens under packet loss, and where protocol-level latency or head-of-line blocking comes from.

topics.title: TCP congestion control algorithms
topics.summary: TCP congestion control adjusts send rate based on acknowledgements, loss, and inferred network capacity. A clear answer mentions slow start, congestion avoidance, multiplicative decrease, RTT, packet loss, and fairness.

topics.title: TLS 1.3 handshake internals
topics.summary: TLS 1.3 reduces handshake round trips and encrypts more of the negotiation than TLS 1.2. Key concepts are ClientHello, key share, certificate verification, Finished messages, forward secrecy, and optional 0-RTT replay risk.

topics.title: HTTP/2 multiplexing & HPACK
topics.summary: HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection and compresses headers with HPACK dynamic tables. It removes HTTP/1.1 request queueing but can still suffer TCP-level head-of-line blocking.

topics.title: HTTP/3 + QUIC packet loss recovery
topics.summary: HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP, combining TLS 1.3, multiplexed streams, connection migration, and per-stream loss recovery. Packet loss no longer blocks unrelated streams the same way HTTP/2 over TCP can.

topics.title: Connection pooling pitfalls
topics.summary: Connection pools reduce setup cost but can fail through exhaustion, stale sockets, head-of-line blocking, uneven load, leaks, or pool sizes that exceed database/server limits. Correct sizing and timeout behavior matter.

topics.title: gRPC streaming + flow control
topics.summary: gRPC streaming sends multiple messages over HTTP/2 streams with flow control. A good explanation covers client/server/bidirectional streams, backpressure, message framing, deadlines, cancellation, and per-stream windows.

groups.name: Deployment and reliability patterns
groups.note: Use this group to keep systems available while code, traffic, dependencies, and failure modes change.

topics.title: Zero-downtime deployment strategies
topics.summary: Zero-downtime deployment keeps traffic served while replacing code. Common techniques include readiness probes, draining, blue-green, canary, backward-compatible schemas, feature flags, and fast rollback.

topics.title: Circuit breaker + bulkhead patterns
topics.summary: Circuit breakers stop calling failing dependencies temporarily; bulkheads isolate resource pools so one failing area does not exhaust the entire service. Together they prevent cascading failures.

topics.title: Database failover & split-brain prevention
topics.summary: Failover promotes a standby when primary fails; split-brain occurs when multiple primaries accept writes. Prevention uses quorum, fencing tokens, leases, STONITH-style isolation, and conservative promotion rules.

topics.title: Blue-green vs canary deployments
topics.summary: Blue-green switches traffic between two full environments; canary gradually shifts a small percentage to a new version. Blue-green is simpler rollback, while canary gives safer progressive exposure.

topics.title: Feature flags with rollout strategies
topics.summary: Feature flags decouple deploy from release and allow targeting, gradual rollout, kill switches, and experiments. Good systems need stable bucketing, auditability, cleanup, and dependency management.

groups.name: Databases, storage, and transactions
groups.note: Use this group to connect correctness guarantees to indexes, query plans, isolation, locks, replication, and storage-engine behavior.

topics.title: Database transaction isolation levels (serializable vs snapshot)
topics.summary: Isolation levels define which concurrent transaction anomalies are possible. Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a consistent view but can allow write skew; serializable aims to behave as if transactions ran one at a time.

topics.title: B-tree vs LSM-tree index internals
topics.summary: B-trees maintain ordered pages for efficient point and range reads, while LSM-trees buffer writes and compact sorted files later. The trade-off is read amplification versus write throughput and compaction cost.

topics.title: Query planner & cost-based optimization
topics.summary: A cost-based query planner estimates alternative execution plans using statistics, selectivity, join order, index availability, and I/O/CPU costs. Bad stats or parameter skew can produce poor plans.

topics.title: Deadlock detection & prevention
topics.summary: Deadlocks occur when transactions wait on each other in a cycle. Databases detect cycles in wait-for graphs or prevent them with lock ordering, timeouts, smaller transactions, and consistent access patterns.

topics.title: ACID vs BASE trade-offs
topics.summary: ACID emphasizes atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability; BASE accepts softer consistency for availability and scalability. The real decision is which invariants must be immediately correct versus eventually reconciled.

topics.title: Sharding strategies & hot partition avoidance
topics.summary: Sharding splits data across partitions by key, range, hash, tenant, or geography. Hot partitions happen when too much traffic targets one shard and are mitigated with better keys, salting, splitting, and load-aware routing.

topics.title: Read replicas lag monitoring
topics.summary: Read replica lag is the delay between primary writes and replica visibility. Monitoring should track replication position/time lag and route read-your-writes or critical reads to fresh sources when needed.

topics.title: Database connection pool exhaustion
topics.summary: Pool exhaustion occurs when all DB connections are busy or leaked. Symptoms include request pileups, timeouts, and cascading latency; fixes include smaller transactions, timeouts, queue limits, and right-sized pools.

topics.title: Prepared statement caching
topics.summary: Prepared statement caching reuses parsed/planned SQL statements to reduce overhead and improve safety. Pitfalls include unbounded caches, schema changes, connection-specific state, and bad generic plans.

topics.title: Index bloat & vacuum strategies
topics.summary: Index bloat is wasted index space from dead or outdated entries, common in MVCC systems. Vacuuming, autovacuum tuning, fillfactor choices, and periodic reindexing control space and planner quality.

groups.name: Distributed systems and consistency
groups.note: Use this group to reason about partitions, locks, consensus, conflict resolution, idempotency, and exactly-once claims.

topics.title: Two-phase commit vs Saga pattern
topics.summary: Two-phase commit coordinates participants for atomic commit but can block and depends on a coordinator. Sagas split work into local transactions with compensating actions, trading atomicity for availability and explicit recovery.

topics.title: Distributed locking (Redlock pitfalls)
topics.summary: Distributed locks are hard because clocks, partitions, pauses, and delayed clients can violate mutual exclusion. Redlock-style leases need careful TTL assumptions and often require fencing tokens to protect downstream resources.

topics.title: CAP theorem in practice
topics.summary: CAP says that during a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability. In practice, systems make per-operation trade-offs with leader routing, quorum reads/writes, retries, and degraded modes.

topics.title: CRDTs & conflict-free replicated data types
topics.summary: CRDTs let replicas update independently and merge deterministically without coordination. Backend use cases include counters, sets, presence, collaborative state, and eventually consistent multi-region writes.

topics.title: Eventual consistency anti-patterns
topics.summary: Eventual consistency becomes an anti-pattern when product flows require immediate guarantees but the system hides lag. Examples include stale permission reads, double spends, missing read-your-writes, and silent conflict overwrites.

topics.title: Idempotency keys in API design
topics.summary: Idempotency keys let clients safely retry state-changing requests without creating duplicate side effects. The server stores the key, request fingerprint, status, and response for a defined retention window.

topics.title: Optimistic locking with version vectors
topics.summary: Optimistic locking detects conflicts by comparing a version or vector before write commit. Version vectors track causal progress across replicas and can distinguish stale writes from concurrent writes.

topics.title: Paxos / Raft consensus internals
topics.summary: Consensus protocols let distributed nodes agree on ordered state despite failures. Raft explains this through leader election, terms, logs, majorities, commit indexes, and safety rules.

topics.title: Byzantine fault tolerance basics
topics.summary: Byzantine fault tolerance handles nodes that can lie, collude, or behave arbitrarily. Classic BFT requires more replicas than crash fault tolerance, commonly 3f+1 replicas to tolerate f Byzantine faults.

topics.title: Exactly-once processing guarantees
topics.summary: Exactly-once usually means effects are applied once through idempotency and transactions, not that messages are delivered once. Strong answers distinguish delivery, processing, side effects, offsets, and sink commits.

groups.name: Messaging, streams, and event-driven systems
groups.note: Use this group to design event pipelines that survive retries, reordering, backpressure, projection lag, and consumer failures.

topics.title: Kafka partition rebalancing & exactly-once semantics
topics.summary: Kafka rebalancing moves partitions across consumers when group membership changes, causing pauses and offset coordination. Exactly-once semantics rely on idempotent producers, transactions, committed offsets, and careful sink behavior.

topics.title: RabbitMQ dead-letter queues & message ordering
topics.summary: RabbitMQ dead-letter queues capture rejected, expired, or failed messages for later handling. Ordering can be broken by retries, multiple consumers, requeueing, priorities, and dead-letter routing.

topics.title: Message-driven architecture (Akka / Orleans)
topics.summary: Message-driven architecture structures systems around asynchronous messages and handlers. It improves decoupling and resilience but introduces delivery guarantees, ordering, retries, idempotency, and observability requirements.

topics.title: CQRS + Event Sourcing projections
topics.summary: CQRS separates command writes from query reads, and event sourcing records state changes as events. Projections build read models from those events and must handle replay, lag, schema changes, and idempotency.

topics.title: Outbox pattern for reliable events
topics.summary: The outbox pattern writes domain data and an event record in the same database transaction, then a relay publishes the event. It avoids losing events between DB commit and broker publish.

topics.title: Background job queues (Celery / BullMQ) retry semantics
topics.summary: Job queues need explicit retry, backoff, dead-letter, timeout, and idempotency semantics. Without them, jobs can duplicate side effects, poison queues, or hide permanent failures behind endless retries.

topics.title: Data pipeline backpressure handling
topics.summary: Pipeline backpressure prevents upstream producers from overwhelming downstream consumers. It is implemented with bounded queues, credits, pull-based reads, pause/resume, rate limits, and load shedding.

topics.title: Idempotent consumers in event streams
topics.summary: Idempotent consumers handle duplicate events safely by recording processed IDs, using natural keys, checking versions, or making writes commutative. This is required because retries and rebalances can redeliver messages.

groups.name: API design, auth, and edge controls
groups.note: Use this group to make APIs safe, compatible, observable, throttled, cacheable, and resilient under N+1, auth, schema, or gateway pressure.

topics.title: GraphQL resolver batching & N+1 problem
topics.group: API design, auth, and edge controls
topics.summary: The GraphQL N+1 problem happens when nested resolvers issue one backend query per parent object. Batching and caching loaders group keys per tick or request to reduce queries while preserving resolver composition.

topics.title: OAuth2 token introspection vs JWT validation
topics.group: API design, auth, and edge controls
topics.summary: JWT validation checks signed claims locally, while token introspection asks the authorization server whether a token is active. JWTs reduce latency but are harder to revoke instantly; introspection centralizes truth but adds network dependency.

topics.title: Rate limiting algorithms (token bucket vs leaky bucket)
topics.group: API design, auth, and edge controls
topics.summary: Token bucket allows bursts up to bucket capacity while refilling over time; leaky bucket smooths output at a fixed rate. The right choice depends on burst tolerance, fairness, and user experience.

topics.title: API gateway throttling & caching layers
topics.group: API design, auth, and edge controls
topics.summary: API gateways enforce cross-cutting policies such as auth, rate limits, request validation, caching, and routing. Caching must vary on identity, authorization, headers, and query shape to avoid data leaks.

topics.title: API contract testing (Pact / Spring Cloud Contract)
topics.group: API design, auth, and edge controls
topics.summary: Contract testing verifies that providers and consumers agree on request/response behavior. It catches breaking changes earlier than full integration tests and supports independent service deployment.

topics.title: Backward-compatible schema evolution
topics.group: API design, auth, and edge controls
topics.summary: Backward-compatible schema evolution changes APIs or events without breaking old consumers. Common moves are additive fields, default values, tolerant readers, deprecation windows, and dual-read/write migrations.

topics.title: Protobuf vs JSON performance trade-offs
topics.group: API design, auth, and edge controls
topics.summary: Protobuf is compact, typed, and schema-driven; JSON is human-readable and ubiquitous. Trade-offs include payload size, CPU parse cost, compatibility rules, introspection, tooling, and browser/debug ergonomics.

groups.name: Observability and operations
groups.note: Use this group to make production behavior debuggable with traces, logs, metrics, cardinality control, sampling, and chaos experiments.

topics.title: Observability: OpenTelemetry tracing propagation
topics.summary: Tracing propagation carries trace and span context across service boundaries. OpenTelemetry standardizes context extraction/injection so logs, metrics, and spans can be correlated across distributed requests.

topics.title: Prometheus metric cardinality explosion
topics.summary: Cardinality explosion happens when labels create too many unique time series. User IDs, raw URLs, emails, request IDs, and high-cardinality dimensions can make Prometheus expensive or unusable.

topics.title: Log aggregation with sampling
topics.summary: Log sampling reduces volume while preserving important signals. Good policies keep all errors/security events, sample noisy success paths, and attach trace IDs so sampled logs still join a request story.

topics.title: Chaos engineering principles
topics.summary: Chaos engineering tests resilience by injecting controlled failures into production-like systems. It should start with hypotheses, blast-radius limits, rollback, observability, and learning from the result.

topics.title: Microservices observability (distributed tracing)
topics.summary: Distributed tracing follows one request across services, queues, and databases. It requires context propagation, span naming discipline, sampling, baggage caution, and correlation with logs and metrics.

groups.name: Runtime, OS, and performance engineering
groups.note: Use this group to reason about memory, CPU, syscalls, worker pools, event loops, atomics, lock-free algorithms, and zero-copy paths.

topics.title: Memory-mapped files vs traditional I/O
topics.summary: Memory-mapped files map file pages into process address space, letting the OS page data in lazily. Traditional I/O copies through explicit buffers. Node does not expose mmap directly, so streams and buffers are the usual tools.

topics.title: Garbage collection tuning (G1 vs ZGC)
topics.summary: G1 and ZGC are JVM collectors with different pause/throughput trade-offs; in Node the analogous topic is V8 heap sizing and GC behavior. Strong explanations separate allocation rate, live set, pause time, and throughput.

topics.title: Thread pools vs virtual threads (Project Loom)
topics.summary: Thread pools bound scarce OS threads; virtual threads multiplex many blocking-style tasks onto fewer carrier threads in the JVM. In Node, the closest contrast is async I/O plus worker threads for CPU-bound work.

topics.title: Actor model vs shared-memory concurrency
topics.summary: The actor model isolates state behind message queues, while shared-memory concurrency shares mutable state with locks or atomics. Actors simplify reasoning but require backpressure and message ordering design.

topics.title: Binary protocol parsing
topics.summary: Binary protocol parsing reads structured fields from byte buffers using offsets, endianness, lengths, and framing rules. Correct parsers defend against partial frames, oversized lengths, and malicious input.

topics.title: Zero-copy networking (sendfile)
topics.summary: Zero-copy networking avoids copying file data through user-space buffers, often with sendfile-like kernel paths. Node typically approximates this with efficient streams, though true sendfile exposure depends on runtime/platform.

topics.title: epoll / kqueue internals
topics.summary: epoll and kqueue are OS event notification mechanisms for scalable nonblocking I/O. Node relies on libuv abstractions over these primitives to drive sockets, timers, and file events.

topics.title: Syscall overhead & context switching
topics.summary: System calls and context switches cross boundaries between user space, kernel space, and runnable tasks. Batching, buffering, async I/O, and fewer tiny writes reduce overhead.

topics.title: Memory barriers & CPU cache coherence
topics.summary: Memory barriers constrain how CPU cores reorder reads/writes so shared-memory programs observe safe ordering. In JavaScript, Atomics operations on SharedArrayBuffer provide the relevant synchronization primitives.

topics.title: Lock-free data structures
topics.summary: Lock-free data structures use atomic operations instead of mutexes so system-wide progress continues even if one thread stalls. They are hard to design because of ABA, memory ordering, and contention.

topics.title: Virtual memory & page faults impact
topics.summary: Virtual memory lets processes use address spaces backed by physical memory and disk. Page faults occur when needed pages are not resident, causing latency from allocation, disk, or OS bookkeeping.

groups.name: Cloud, containers, and service topology
groups.note: Use this group to model platform primitives like service meshes, discovery, sidecars, serverless, Kubernetes disruption controls, and container hardening.

topics.title: Kubernetes pod disruption budgets
topics.summary: Pod disruption budgets limit voluntary disruptions so enough replicas remain available during drains, upgrades, or maintenance. They are useful only when paired with enough replicas, readiness probes, and capacity.

topics.title: Service mesh traffic shifting
topics.summary: Service mesh traffic shifting routes percentages of traffic between versions or services using proxy control planes. It supports canary, blue-green, retries, and mTLS, but adds latency, complexity, and debugging surface.

topics.title: Serverless cold-start mitigation
topics.summary: Cold starts happen when a serverless runtime initializes before handling a request. Mitigation includes smaller bundles, hoisted clients, lazy initialization, provisioned concurrency, and avoiding heavy startup work.

topics.title: Container runtime security (seccomp, AppArmor)
topics.summary: Container runtime security restricts what a process can do despite sharing the host kernel. seccomp filters syscalls, AppArmor/SELinux constrain access, and least-privilege settings reduce blast radius.

topics.title: Sidecar pattern limitations
topics.summary: Sidecars add colocated helper processes for proxying, logging, security, or config. Limitations include extra hops, resource overhead, lifecycle coupling, harder debugging, and duplicated functionality per pod.

topics.title: Service discovery (Consul vs DNS)
topics.summary: Service discovery maps logical service names to healthy instances. DNS is simple and ubiquitous; Consul-style systems can add health checks, metadata, watches, and stronger service catalog semantics.

groups.name: Caching, hashing, and approximate data structures
groups.note: Use this group to design fast paths that remain correct enough under invalidation, shard movement, cardinality estimation, and hot-key pressure.

topics.title: Distributed cache invalidation (cache-aside vs write-through)
topics.group: Caching, hashing, and approximate data structures
topics.summary: Cache-aside loads on miss and invalidates after writes; write-through writes cache and database together. Distributed invalidation must handle races, partial failures, versioning, and cross-node propagation delay.

topics.title: Eventual consistency in cache
topics.group: Caching, hashing, and approximate data structures
topics.summary: Eventually consistent caches can serve stale data after writes, invalidations, or replication delays. Safe design scopes staleness, uses versions, routes critical reads to truth, and avoids caching irreversible authorization decisions incorrectly.

topics.title: Bloom filters & HyperLogLog in practice
topics.group: Caching, hashing, and approximate data structures
topics.summary: Bloom filters answer maybe-present/definitely-not-present with false positives; HyperLogLog estimates cardinality with small memory. Both trade exactness for speed and memory efficiency.

topics.title: Consistent hashing for load balancing
topics.group: Caching, hashing, and approximate data structures
topics.summary: Consistent hashing maps keys to nodes so adding or removing nodes moves only a fraction of keys. It is useful for caches, shards, and load balancing with reduced remapping churn.

groups.name: Design process and trade-offs
groups.note: Use this group to turn product goals into explicit requirements, constraints, trade-offs, and decisions that can be revisited later.

topics.title: Functional vs non-functional requirements
topics.summary: Functional requirements describe what the system must do, while non-functional requirements describe qualities such as latency, availability, privacy, durability, scale, and cost. Senior design work makes both explicit before choosing components.

topics.title: SLOs and error budgets
topics.summary: SLOs define target reliability for user-visible behavior, while error budgets quantify how much unreliability the system can spend. They turn vague reliability goals into decisions about release pace, alerting, redundancy, and degradation.

groups.name: Scale, capacity, and latency
groups.note: Use this group to size traffic, storage, throughput, latency budgets, queues, caches, and concurrency before selecting technology.

topics.title: Capacity estimation
topics.summary: Capacity estimation turns traffic, payload size, storage retention, fanout, and peak multipliers into concrete throughput and storage numbers. The goal is not perfect prediction; it is making bottlenecks and scaling assumptions visible.

topics.title: Latency budget decomposition
topics.summary: A latency budget splits an end-to-end target across client work, network hops, edge logic, services, databases, queues, and third-party calls. It helps identify where parallelism, caching, streaming, or simplification is required.

groups.name: Boundaries and topology
groups.note: Use this group to place client, edge, API, service, data, control-plane, and data-plane responsibilities deliberately.

topics.title: Client-edge-service boundaries
topics.summary: Client, edge, and service boundaries decide where validation, personalization, caching, rendering, authorization, and aggregation live. Good boundaries reduce latency and coupling without leaking trusted responsibilities to untrusted environments.
related: Backend: API gateway throttling and caching layers

topics.title: API gateway and BFF boundaries
topics.summary: An API gateway applies cross-cutting concerns such as auth, rate limits, caching, and routing, while a backend-for-frontend shapes APIs around a specific client experience. Mixing them carelessly can create a slow, overloaded coordination layer.
related: Backend: API gateway throttling and caching layers

topics.title: Read path vs write path design
topics.summary: Read paths and write paths often need different guarantees, storage models, caches, and scaling strategies. Separating them clarifies which flows require immediate correctness and which can tolerate projection lag or denormalized views.

topics.title: Control plane vs data plane
topics.summary: The control plane configures policy and desired state, while the data plane handles the high-volume request or data path. Separating them keeps runtime traffic fast and resilient even when management workflows are slower or partially unavailable.
related: Backend: Feature flags with rollout strategies

groups.name: Data, consistency, and workflows
groups.note: Use this group to connect access patterns, consistency needs, partitions, freshness, events, and workflow recovery into one design.

topics.title: Data modeling from access patterns
topics.summary: Access-pattern-first data modeling starts with queries, writes, cardinality, ordering, and consistency needs before choosing tables, documents, indexes, or streams. It prevents elegant schemas that cannot serve real traffic.
related: Backend: Query planner and cost-based optimization
Backend: B-tree vs LSM-tree index internals

topics.title: Cache placement and invalidation
topics.summary: Cache placement decides whether data is cached in the browser, edge, gateway, service, database layer, or client state. Invalidation must match freshness requirements, user specificity, mutation flow, and failure behavior.

topics.title: Partitioning and tenant isolation
topics.summary: Partitioning splits data and traffic across shards, tenants, regions, or cells. Tenant isolation adds blast-radius control so one large or unhealthy tenant does not degrade unrelated customers.
related: Backend: Consistent hashing for load balancing

topics.title: Read freshness routing
topics.summary: Read freshness routing chooses between replicas, caches, primaries, or quorum reads based on how fresh a response must be. It is the system-level version of making read-your-writes and stale-data rules explicit.

topics.title: Async workflow design
topics.summary: Async workflow design coordinates durable state changes across queues, jobs, events, retries, and compensations. The design must define ownership, idempotency, retry semantics, visibility, and recovery after partial progress.
related: Backend: Outbox pattern for reliable events
Backend: Background job queues retry semantics

groups.name: Reliability and operations
groups.note: Use this group to reason about failure modes, overload behavior, fallback, disaster recovery, observability, alerts, and releases.

topics.title: Failure mode analysis
topics.summary: Failure mode analysis lists what can break, how the system detects it, what user impact it creates, and which mitigation applies. It converts architecture diagrams from happy-path pictures into operable designs.

topics.title: Backpressure and load shedding
topics.summary: Backpressure slows producers when downstream systems are saturated, while load shedding rejects or drops work deliberately to preserve critical paths. A design should define queue limits, priorities, retry rules, and user-visible errors.

topics.title: Degradation and fallback design
topics.summary: Degradation and fallback design decides which features can be disabled, simplified, cached, or delayed when dependencies fail. Good fallbacks are intentional product states, not accidental error handling.

topics.title: Disaster recovery objectives (RTO/RPO)
topics.summary: RTO is how long recovery may take, and RPO is how much data loss is acceptable. These objectives drive backup frequency, replication, failover automation, drills, and whether the design needs active-active or active-passive recovery.
related: Backend: Database failover and split-brain prevention

topics.title: Operational readiness review
topics.summary: Operational readiness checks whether a system can be deployed, observed, rolled back, debugged, scaled, secured, and supported before it handles real traffic. It is the practical bridge between design and production ownership.

topics.title: Tracing across async workflows
topics.summary: Tracing across async workflows carries correlation through requests, events, jobs, retries, and projections. Without it, the system can appear healthy while individual user workflows disappear between components.

topics.title: Runbook and alert design
topics.summary: Runbook and alert design connects symptoms to ownership, impact, first checks, mitigation, and escalation. Alerts should be tied to user impact or fast-burn risk, not every noisy internal metric.

topics.title: Release strategy selection
topics.summary: Release strategy selection chooses between rolling, blue-green, canary, feature flags, shadow traffic, and migrations based on blast radius, reversibility, data compatibility, and confidence signals.
related: Backend: Feature flags with rollout strategies

groups.name: Security, abuse, and governance
groups.note: Use this group to protect system boundaries, secrets, tenants, quotas, abuse paths, and operational policy surfaces.

topics.title: Threat modeling at system boundaries
topics.summary: Threat modeling at system boundaries identifies trust zones, entry points, assets, attackers, and mitigations. It keeps security connected to architecture instead of treating it as a checklist after implementation.
related: Backend: OAuth2 token introspection vs JWT validation

topics.title: Abuse and quota controls
topics.summary: Abuse and quota controls protect systems from spam, scraping, brute force, runaway automation, and unfair resource use. Effective designs combine identity, rate limits, quotas, anomaly detection, and appeal paths.
related: Backend: API gateway throttling and caching layers

topics.title: Secret and configuration boundaries
topics.summary: Secret and configuration boundaries define where credentials, feature flags, tenant settings, and runtime policy may live. A safe design prevents secrets from leaking to clients, logs, traces, build artifacts, or untrusted plugins.

groups.name: Cost, evolution, and decision records
groups.note: Use this group to keep architecture economically grounded and evolvable through buy/build calls, migrations, and recorded decisions.

topics.title: Cost-aware architecture
topics.summary: Cost-aware architecture models the cost drivers of traffic, storage, compute, egress, third-party APIs, observability, and operational effort. It does not mean choosing the cheapest path; it means making cost part of the design trade-off.

topics.title: Build vs buy evaluation
topics.summary: Build vs buy evaluation compares capability fit, integration risk, lock-in, security, operations, support, cost curves, and strategic differentiation. The useful answer is often a staged decision, not a permanent ideology.

topics.title: Migration and strangler patterns
topics.summary: Migration and strangler patterns replace systems incrementally by routing slices of traffic or capability to the new path while the old path keeps running. The design must include parity checks, rollback, data sync, and ownership boundaries.

topics.title: Architecture decision records
topics.summary: Architecture decision records capture context, decision, alternatives, consequences, and revisit triggers. They preserve the reasoning behind trade-offs so future engineers can change direction without rediscovering old constraints.
related: Frontend: Frontend architecture and rendering models

groups.name: LLM fundamentals and model behavior
groups.note: Use this group to understand how model limits, sampling, latency, throughput, and capability fit affect production AI features.

topics.title: Tokens and context windows
topics.summary: Tokens are the model's input and output units, and the context window is the bounded working set the model can attend to. Practical AI engineering treats context as a scarce budget shared by instructions, user input, retrieved sources, tools, and output.

topics.title: Sampling, temperature, and top-p
topics.summary: Sampling settings change how the model chooses among likely next tokens. Temperature affects sharpness, top-p limits the candidate probability mass, and both must be tuned around task type, determinism needs, and evaluation signals.
related: System Design: SLOs and error budgets

topics.title: Model capability fit
topics.summary: Model capability fit matches a task to a model based on reasoning depth, tool use, latency, context length, language coverage, multimodal needs, cost, and safety behavior. The best model is the one that meets the product constraint, not always the largest model.
related: System Design: Build vs buy evaluation
