topics.title: Latency, throughput, and batching
topics.summary: AI latency includes queueing, prompt assembly, model time, streaming cadence, tool calls, and post-processing. Throughput work often introduces batching or caching, which must be balanced against tail latency and personalization.

groups.name: Prompting and context engineering
groups.note: Use this group to assemble instructions, variables, examples, source context, and conversation state without losing control of the task.

topics.title: Instruction hierarchy
topics.summary: Instruction hierarchy defines which instructions outrank others, such as system policy, developer intent, tool constraints, retrieved content, and user requests. It is the foundation for keeping model behavior stable when context contains conflicting text.
related: System Design: Threat modeling at system boundaries

topics.title: Prompt templates and variables
topics.summary: Prompt templates separate fixed instructions from dynamic variables, making prompts easier to test, version, localize, and audit. Safe templates escape or delimit untrusted inputs so data is not confused with instructions.

topics.title: Context pruning and summarization
topics.summary: Context pruning chooses what to keep, compress, or drop as a conversation or task grows. Good pruning preserves goals, constraints, current state, source citations, and unresolved decisions instead of blindly keeping recent messages.
related: System Design: Data modeling from access patterns

topics.title: Few-shot examples
topics.summary: Few-shot examples demonstrate the target input-output pattern inside the prompt. They are most useful when they cover edge cases, failure modes, tone, structure, or domain-specific transformations that plain instructions underspecify.

groups.name: Structured outputs and tool use
groups.note: Use this group to make model interactions machine-checkable with schemas, tool contracts, validation, dispatch, and permission boundaries.

topics.title: JSON schema constrained output
topics.summary: Schema-constrained output makes model responses machine-checkable by defining required fields, types, enums, arrays, and nesting. It reduces parser fragility, but downstream code must still validate and handle refusals or partial failures.

topics.title: Tool calling contracts
topics.summary: Tool calling contracts define the names, arguments, permissions, side effects, return values, and error semantics of tools the model may request. Strong contracts keep the model as a planner while application code remains the executor.
related: System Design: Secret and configuration boundaries

topics.title: Tool dispatch and validation
topics.summary: Tool dispatch maps model-requested tool calls to allowed application functions after validating tool name, arguments, permissions, and expected side effects. Dispatch code is a security boundary, not just plumbing.
related: Backend: OAuth2 token introspection vs JWT validation

topics.title: Tool permission boundaries
topics.summary: Tool permission boundaries restrict what the model can cause the system to read, write, spend, send, delete, or expose. Permission should be based on user authorization, task context, tool risk, and confirmation requirements.
related: System Design: Threat modeling at system boundaries
System Design: Secret and configuration boundaries

groups.name: Retrieval and knowledge grounding
groups.note: Use this group to connect embeddings, chunking, metadata, retrieval, reranking, and source-of-truth rules into grounded answers.

topics.title: Embeddings and cosine similarity
topics.summary: Embeddings map text or other content into vectors so semantic similarity can be searched. Cosine similarity is a common scoring method, but retrieval quality also depends on chunking, metadata, filters, freshness, and reranking.
related: System Design: Data modeling from access patterns

topics.title: Chunking and metadata strategy
topics.summary: Chunking splits source material into retrieval units, while metadata carries source, ownership, freshness, access control, hierarchy, and document structure. Bad chunking can make good embeddings look weak.
related: System Design: Data modeling from access patterns

topics.title: RAG retrieval pipeline
topics.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation pulls relevant source material into model context before generation. A production RAG pipeline includes indexing, filtering, retrieval, reranking, source packing, answer generation, and citation or grounding checks.
related: Backend: Query planner and cost-based optimization

topics.title: Reranking and hybrid search
topics.summary: Reranking reorders retrieved candidates using a stronger relevance signal, while hybrid search combines lexical and vector retrieval. These techniques improve grounding when semantic search alone misses exact terms, IDs, or rare phrases.
related: Backend: Query planner and cost-based optimization

topics.title: Conversation memory vs source of truth
topics.summary: Conversation memory is the model-facing summary of interaction state, while the source of truth is the durable system record. Designs should avoid letting generated summaries silently overwrite authoritative data.
related: System Design: Read path vs write path design

groups.name: Evaluation and observability
groups.note: Use this group to measure AI behavior with datasets, traces, prompt regression tests, judge calibration, and production quality signals.

topics.title: Golden set evals
topics.summary: Golden set evals use curated examples with expected behavior to measure prompt, model, retrieval, and tool changes. Good sets include common cases, edge cases, regressions, and unacceptable outputs.

topics.title: LLM-as-judge pitfalls
topics.summary: LLM-as-judge evals can scale qualitative review, but judges have bias, drift, prompt sensitivity, and blind spots. They need calibration against human labels, clear rubrics, disagreement tracking, and spot checks.
related: System Design: SLOs and error budgets

topics.title: Trace logging for AI features
topics.summary: AI traces record prompts, model choices, tool calls, retrieval inputs, outputs, latency, cost, and policy decisions with sensitive data controls. They are required to debug quality regressions and production incidents.
related: System Design: Tracing across async workflows

topics.title: Prompt regression testing
topics.summary: Prompt regression testing checks that prompt, model, tool, or retrieval changes do not break known behavior. The useful unit is the whole AI interaction contract, not just prompt text.

groups.name: Safety, security, and data handling
groups.note: Use this group to reduce prompt injection, unsafe output, privacy leakage, and unclear escalation behavior in AI-backed systems.

topics.title: Prompt injection defense
topics.summary: Prompt injection defense treats retrieved content, web pages, documents, and user text as untrusted data that may contain instructions. Defenses include instruction hierarchy, source isolation, tool permission checks, allowlists, and confirmation gates.
related: System Design: Threat modeling at system boundaries

topics.title: Output guardrails
topics.summary: Output guardrails validate model responses before display, execution, storage, or sending. They can enforce schema, policy, unsafe-content checks, citation requirements, numeric bounds, or human review.

topics.title: PII redaction and data minimization
topics.summary: PII redaction and data minimization reduce sensitive data exposure in prompts, logs, traces, evals, and vendor calls. The safest token is the one never sent, logged, or retained unnecessarily.
related: System Design: Secret and configuration boundaries

topics.title: Refusal and escalation paths
topics.summary: Refusal and escalation paths define what the product does when the model cannot safely or confidently complete a request. Good designs preserve user trust with clear alternatives, support handoff, or constrained partial help.
related: System Design: Degradation and fallback design

groups.name: Agentic workflows
groups.note: Use this group to design loops that plan, act, observe, persist state, ask for human review, and recover from partial progress.

topics.title: Agent loop design
topics.summary: An agent loop repeatedly observes state, decides next action, calls tools, records results, and stops when the goal is complete or blocked. The hard parts are stopping criteria, state, permissions, retries, and recovery.

topics.title: Plan-execute-observe cycles
topics.summary: Plan-execute-observe cycles split agent work into an explicit plan, bounded actions, and evidence-based updates. They help keep long tasks auditable and prevent the agent from drifting away from the objective.

topics.title: Human-in-the-loop checkpoints
topics.summary: Human-in-the-loop checkpoints pause an AI workflow before high-risk actions, ambiguous decisions, expensive operations, or irreversible side effects. They should be placed by risk, not sprinkled everywhere.
related: System Design: Abuse and quota controls
System Design: Secret and configuration boundaries

topics.title: Long-running task state
topics.summary: Long-running task state stores objective, plan, decisions, tool results, unresolved blockers, budgets, and verification evidence. Without durable state, agent workflows become hard to resume, audit, or debug.

groups.name: Model operations, cost, and rollout
groups.note: Use this group to route models, control cost, cache safely, stream responses, and roll out AI features with measurable risk.

topics.title: Model routing and fallback
topics.summary: Model routing sends requests to different models based on task complexity, latency target, cost budget, context size, availability, safety policy, or tenant tier. Fallback should preserve correctness boundaries, not just retry anywhere.
related: System Design: Degradation and fallback design

topics.title: Cost controls and response caching
topics.summary: Cost controls for AI systems include token budgets, model routing, prompt trimming, batch processing, response caching, tenant quotas, and observability. Caching is safest for deterministic, non-user-specific, policy-stable outputs.

topics.title: Streaming AI UX
topics.summary: Streaming AI UX delivers partial output as it is generated, improving perceived latency and enabling cancellation. It must handle partial sentences, tool-call pauses, errors, moderation, and final-state reconciliation.

topics.title: AI feature rollout
topics.summary: AI feature rollout introduces model-backed behavior gradually with flags, eval gates, tracing, human review, fallback, and cost monitoring. Rollout plans should account for quality drift as well as uptime.
related: Backend: Feature flags with rollout strategies

groups.name: Relational modeling and SQL
groups.note: Use this group to design schemas, constraints, query shapes, and relational access patterns that stay understandable as data grows.

topics.title: Relational schema design
topics.summary: Relational schema design maps domain entities, relationships, constraints, and access patterns into tables that can preserve integrity over time. Good design uses keys, constraints, naming, cardinality, and ownership boundaries deliberately.

topics.title: SQL joins and query shape
topics.summary: SQL joins combine rows across tables, but query shape determines cardinality, duplicate rows, filter placement, and whether the database can use indexes. Engineers should explain inner, outer, semi, and anti joins from result semantics first.

topics.title: Normalization vs denormalization
topics.summary: Normalization reduces duplication and update anomalies, while denormalization duplicates data to speed reads or simplify access. The trade-off is correctness and write complexity versus query performance and product latency.

topics.title: Data integrity constraints
topics.summary: Data integrity constraints make correctness durable inside the database through primary keys, foreign keys, unique constraints, checks, not-null rules, and exclusion constraints. They protect invariants even when application code has bugs.

topics.title: Temporal data modeling
topics.summary: Temporal modeling captures when facts are valid, when the system learned them, and how history changes. It matters for auditability, pricing, entitlement windows, late-arriving updates, and reproducible analytics.

groups.name: Indexing and query performance
groups.note: Use this group to connect query plans, index design, statistics, memory, and workload shape to practical performance outcomes.

topics.title: Index selection and covering indexes
topics.summary: Index selection matches workload filters, joins, ordering, uniqueness, and projection columns. Covering indexes can serve a query without visiting base rows, but they increase write cost and storage.

topics.title: Query execution plan reading
topics.summary: Query plans show how the database intends to scan, join, sort, aggregate, and estimate row counts. Reading plans helps diagnose missing indexes, stale statistics, bad join order, and memory-heavy operations.

topics.title: Statistics and cardinality estimation
topics.summary: Statistics and cardinality estimates let a planner compare possible execution paths. Bad estimates from skew, correlation, stale stats, or parameter sensitivity can make reasonable SQL run poorly.

topics.title: Connection pool sizing
topics.summary: Connection pool sizing balances application concurrency against database capacity. Too few connections bottleneck callers; too many cause queueing, memory pressure, lock contention, and database overload.

topics.title: Hot query and slow query triage
topics.summary: Hot query triage identifies the queries that dominate database load by frequency, latency, rows scanned, lock wait, and memory use. Fixes can include index changes, query rewrites, caching, pagination, or product flow changes.

groups.name: Transactions, migrations, and integrity
groups.note: Use this group to protect correctness while schema, code, data volume, and concurrent writes change.

topics.title: Transaction boundary design
topics.summary: Transaction boundary design decides which reads and writes must commit atomically, how long locks are held, and what invariants need isolation. Boundaries that are too wide hurt concurrency; too narrow leak partial state.

topics.title: Schema migration expand-contract
topics.summary: Expand-contract migrations introduce schema changes in backward-compatible phases: expand, dual-read/write or backfill, cut over, then contract. This keeps old and new code safe during rolling deploys.

topics.title: Online backfills
topics.summary: Online backfills update existing data while production traffic continues. Safe backfills use batches, checkpoints, idempotency, throttling, observability, and rollback or pause behavior.

topics.title: Optimistic concurrency control
topics.summary: Optimistic concurrency control detects conflicting writes with versions, timestamps, compare-and-swap, or conditional updates. It works well when conflicts are rare and retry behavior is explicit.

topics.title: Idempotent data writes
topics.summary: Idempotent writes make retries safe by using stable operation IDs, uniqueness constraints, upserts, or processed-event tables. They are essential when clients, workers, or queues can repeat work.

groups.name: Storage topology and replication
groups.note: Use this group to reason about partitioning, replicas, backups, search indexes, time-series storage, and tenant boundaries.

topics.title: Partitioning and sharding strategy
topics.summary: Partitioning and sharding split data by tenant, key, hash, range, geography, or workload. A good strategy minimizes hot partitions, cross-shard joins, rebalancing pain, and tenant blast radius.

topics.title: Replication lag and read scaling
topics.summary: Read replicas increase read capacity but introduce freshness lag and failover complexity. Designs must define which reads can be stale, how lag is measured, and when to route to the primary.

topics.title: Backup, restore, and point-in-time recovery
topics.summary: Backups only matter if restores are tested. Point-in-time recovery combines base backups and logs to restore to a chosen moment, bounded by RPO, RTO, retention, and access controls.

topics.title: Search indexing and relevance
topics.summary: Search indexing transforms source records into searchable documents with tokenization, ranking signals, filters, facets, and freshness rules. Search is a derived data system that needs sync and repair paths.

topics.title: Time-series data modeling
topics.summary: Time-series modeling optimizes append-heavy measurements with timestamps, tags, retention, rollups, downsampling, and query windows. It is common in observability, IoT, billing, and analytics.

groups.name: Analytics, pipelines, and governance
groups.note: Use this group to move data into analytical systems with clear semantics, quality checks, lineage, and retention rules.

topics.title: OLTP vs OLAP system choice
topics.summary: OLTP systems optimize transactional correctness and low-latency writes, while OLAP systems optimize analytical scans and aggregations. Mixing them without boundaries can hurt both product behavior and reporting.

topics.title: CDC and event streams
topics.summary: Change data capture turns database changes into ordered event streams for replication, search indexing, analytics, or integration. It must handle ordering, deletes, schema evolution, backfills, and replay.

topics.title: ETL vs ELT pipelines
topics.summary: ETL transforms before loading into the target system, while ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the analytical store. The decision changes cost, lineage, debugging, privacy, and ownership.

topics.title: Warehouse modeling and fact tables
topics.summary: Warehouse modeling organizes analytical data around facts, dimensions, grain, slowly changing dimensions, and business definitions. It keeps reporting consistent across teams and tools.

topics.title: Semantic metrics layer
topics.summary: A semantic metrics layer defines measures, dimensions, filters, windows, and ownership once so dashboards and product analysis agree. It prevents each report from inventing a different version of revenue or active users.

topics.title: Data quality checks
topics.summary: Data quality checks assert freshness, completeness, uniqueness, value ranges, referential integrity, and volume expectations. They catch broken ingestion or product instrumentation before decisions depend on bad data.

topics.title: Deduplication and late-arriving data
topics.summary: Deduplication and late-arriving data handling keep analytical results correct when events are retried, delayed, reordered, or replayed. Designs need stable IDs, watermarks, correction windows, and recomputation paths.

topics.title: Data retention and archival policy
topics.summary: Retention and archival policy define how long data stays hot, warm, cold, anonymized, or deleted. It balances product needs, cost, legal obligations, privacy, and restore expectations.

topics.title: Data lineage and observability
topics.summary: Data lineage and observability show where data came from, how it changed, when it refreshed, and what downstream assets depend on it. They are the operational controls for trusted analytical systems.

topics.title: Vector storage and retrieval
topics.summary: Vector storage supports similarity search over embeddings with indexes, metadata filters, refresh policies, and recall-latency trade-offs. It is useful for AI retrieval, recommendations, duplicate detection, and semantic search.

groups.name: Source control, CI, and release automation
groups.note: Use this group to turn changes into repeatable, reviewable, reversible delivery paths.

topics.title: Git workflow and branch protection
topics.group: Source control, CI, and release automation
topics.summary: Git workflow and branch protection define how changes move from local work to reviewed, tested, mergeable history. Useful controls include required checks, protected branches, signed commits or tags, and review ownership.

topics.title: CI pipeline design
topics.group: Source control, CI, and release automation
topics.summary: CI pipeline design orders checks so fast deterministic failures happen early and expensive integration work runs only when needed. Good pipelines separate install, lint, test, build, package, and artifact verification.

topics.title: Generated artifact drift checks
topics.group: Source control, CI, and release automation
topics.summary: Generated artifact drift checks run the generator in CI and fail when committed generated output is stale. This protects source-of-truth workflows without letting CI silently rewrite reviewed code.

topics.title: Deployment strategy selection
topics.group: Source control, CI, and release automation
topics.summary: Deployment strategy selection chooses rolling, blue-green, canary, shadow, or feature-flagged rollout based on reversibility, data compatibility, blast radius, and signal quality.

topics.title: Rollback and roll-forward planning
topics.group: Source control, CI, and release automation
topics.summary: Rollback and roll-forward planning defines what happens when a release fails. The plan must account for code, config, data migrations, caches, messages, and external side effects.

groups.name: Infrastructure, environments, and cloud networking
groups.note: Use this group to model infrastructure state, environment promotion, DNS, certificates, load balancing, and network reachability.

topics.title: Infrastructure as Code state
topics.summary: Infrastructure as Code state records the known deployed resources and their desired configuration. State must be locked, backed up, reviewed, and protected because it is a control surface for production.

topics.title: Environment promotion
topics.summary: Environment promotion moves the same build artifact through development, staging, and production with environment-specific config. It prevents rebuilding different binaries for each environment.

topics.title: Cloud networking basics
topics.summary: Cloud networking basics include VPCs, subnets, routing tables, NAT, firewalls, private endpoints, and service reachability. Platform engineers must reason about packets, identity, and policy together.

topics.title: DNS and certificate operations
topics.summary: DNS and certificate operations keep names resolvable and encrypted endpoints trusted. Practical knowledge includes TTLs, CNAMEs, apex records, ACME renewals, SANs, wildcard certs, and rollout timing.

topics.title: Load balancing and health checks
topics.summary: Load balancing distributes traffic across healthy targets, while health checks decide whether a target should receive traffic. Bad checks can amplify incidents by sending traffic to broken or warming instances.

groups.name: Containers, orchestration, and runtime platforms
groups.note: Use this group to operate workloads with container hygiene, scheduling, autoscaling, service topology, and runtime constraints.

topics.title: Container image build hygiene
topics.summary: Container image hygiene reduces build drift, size, vulnerabilities, and runtime privilege. Good images pin bases, avoid secrets, run as non-root, minimize layers, and separate build tools from runtime.

topics.title: Kubernetes workload primitives
topics.summary: Kubernetes workload primitives such as Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and Ingresses describe desired runtime state. Engineers should know what each primitive owns and does not own.

topics.title: Autoscaling signal selection
topics.summary: Autoscaling signal selection chooses metrics that indicate real demand, such as CPU, memory, queue depth, request concurrency, or custom service latency. Bad signals can scale too late, too far, or in the wrong direction.

topics.title: Service mesh trade-offs
topics.summary: Service meshes add traffic policy, mTLS, retries, telemetry, and routing at the sidecar or proxy layer. They also add operational complexity, resource cost, and debugging paths that teams must be ready to own.

topics.title: Serverless operational constraints
topics.summary: Serverless platforms remove server management but introduce limits around cold starts, execution duration, concurrency, packaging, network access, and observability. The runtime shape must fit the workload.

groups.name: Security, identity, and supply chain
groups.note: Use this group to control secrets, permissions, artifact trust, policy, and blast radius across the platform.

topics.title: Secrets management and rotation
topics.summary: Secrets management controls how credentials are created, stored, injected, rotated, audited, and revoked. Rotation must be designed so old and new credentials can overlap safely.

topics.title: IAM least privilege
topics.summary: IAM least privilege grants only the actions and resources needed for a role. It requires scoping by identity, environment, action, resource, condition, and operational break-glass paths.

topics.title: Supply chain provenance
topics.summary: Supply chain provenance records where artifacts came from, how they were built, and what source revision produced them. It supports auditability, tamper detection, and safer deployment policy.

topics.title: Policy as code
topics.summary: Policy as code evaluates infrastructure, deployment, or access rules automatically before changes land. It makes governance reviewable and testable instead of relying on manual memory.

topics.title: Dependency update automation
topics.summary: Dependency update automation opens reviewed, testable changes for package and action updates. It reduces stale dependency risk but needs grouping, rate limits, lockfile discipline, and CI confidence.

groups.name: Observability, incidents, and operations
groups.note: Use this group to make production ownership measurable, alertable, recoverable, and improvable after incidents.

topics.title: Observability baseline
topics.summary: An observability baseline defines the minimum logs, metrics, traces, dashboards, and service metadata every production service should expose. It lets responders compare systems quickly during incidents.

topics.title: Alert routing and ownership
topics.summary: Alert routing and ownership connect symptoms to responsible teams, escalation policies, runbooks, and user impact. Alerts without owners become noise; owners without context burn out.

topics.title: Incident command and postmortems
topics.summary: Incident command coordinates roles, communication, mitigation, timeline, and follow-up during production incidents. Postmortems turn incidents into system improvements without blame.

topics.title: SLO burn-rate alerting
topics.summary: SLO burn-rate alerting pages when a service consumes its error budget too quickly across short and long windows. It connects alert urgency to user-visible reliability targets.

topics.title: Runbooks and game days
topics.summary: Runbooks document diagnosis and mitigation steps, while game days rehearse failures before real incidents. Together they turn operational knowledge into practiced team behavior.

topics.title: Cost allocation and FinOps
topics.summary: Cost allocation and FinOps connect platform spend to teams, products, environments, and unit economics. Good systems expose cost drivers early enough for engineering decisions to change them.

groups.name: Developer experience and platform product
groups.note: Use this group to build internal platforms, templates, local environments, and APIs that make good engineering paths easy to follow.

topics.title: Internal developer platforms
topics.summary: Internal developer platforms provide paved paths for teams to build, deploy, observe, and operate software. They should be treated as products with users, adoption metrics, support, and feedback loops.

topics.title: Golden paths and service templates
topics.summary: Golden paths and templates encode recommended architecture, CI, deployment, observability, security, and ownership defaults. They reduce repeated decisions without blocking teams that need justified exceptions.

topics.title: Local development environments
topics.summary: Local development environments should make common workflows fast and realistic without requiring production credentials. The design balances fidelity, startup time, dependency weight, and reproducibility.

topics.title: Feature flag operations
topics.summary: Feature flag operations manage targeting, ownership, cleanup, defaults, audit logs, and failure behavior. Without lifecycle discipline, flags become hidden production configuration debt.

topics.title: Configuration management and dynamic rollout
topics.summary: Configuration management separates deploy-time code from runtime policy. Dynamic rollout lets teams change behavior safely, but requires validation, auditability, scoping, rollback, and cache invalidation.

topics.title: Platform API ergonomics
topics.summary: Platform API ergonomics determine how easily product teams can use internal capabilities without learning every underlying system. Good APIs expose safe defaults, clear errors, stable contracts, and escape hatches.

groups.name: IP addressing and routing fundamentals
groups.note: Use this group to reason about address space, route selection, NAT, and global traffic paths before blaming application code.

topics.title: CIDR subnet planning
topics.summary: CIDR subnet planning divides address space into ranges sized for hosts, growth, routing, and isolation. A good plan leaves room for expansion, avoids overlapping ranges, and keeps route tables understandable.

topics.title: Private vs public addressing
topics.summary: Private and public addressing define whether traffic can be routed on the public internet or must stay inside a private network boundary. Engineers should recognize RFC1918 ranges, loopback, link-local addresses, and the translation or proxy paths needed for egress.

topics.title: Route tables and next hops
topics.summary: Route tables choose the next hop for packets based on destination prefixes. Longest-prefix matching, default routes, blackhole routes, and asymmetric paths are core ideas for debugging reachability.

topics.title: NAT and egress design
topics.summary: NAT and egress design let private workloads initiate outbound traffic through shared public addresses. Designs must account for port exhaustion, source identity, logging, allowlists, and failure domains.

topics.title: Anycast and global routing
topics.summary: Anycast advertises the same address from multiple locations so routing sends users to a nearby or preferred site. It improves global latency and resilience but requires careful health signaling and traffic-drain behavior.

groups.name: DNS, TLS, and edge delivery
groups.note: Use this group to connect names, certificates, proxies, CDNs, caches, and edge routing to real production reachability.

topics.title: DNS record types and TTLs
topics.summary: DNS record types and TTLs control how names resolve and how quickly changes propagate. Practical fluency includes A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, CAA, apex constraints, and cache duration trade-offs.

topics.title: Recursive vs authoritative DNS
topics.summary: Recursive resolvers answer client queries by consulting authoritative DNS servers and caching results. Knowing the difference helps diagnose stale answers, delegation mistakes, split-horizon DNS, and resolver-specific failures.

topics.title: TLS certificate chain validation
topics.summary: TLS certificate chain validation proves that a presented certificate chains to a trusted root and matches the requested host. Failures can come from expired certs, missing intermediates, name mismatch, weak policy, or incorrect time.

topics.title: CDN caching and edge routing
topics.summary: CDN caching and edge routing move responses closer to users while respecting cache keys, freshness, purge behavior, origin shielding, and request routing policy. The edge becomes part of the production system, not just a static asset layer.

topics.title: HTTP proxy and reverse proxy behavior
topics.summary: HTTP proxies and reverse proxies terminate, forward, rewrite, buffer, retry, and observe traffic between clients and services. Headers such as Host, X-Forwarded-For, and Forwarded become trust boundaries.

groups.name: Transport protocols and performance
groups.note: Use this group to explain latency, connection setup, packet loss, congestion, MTU behavior, and load-balancing effects.

topics.title: TCP handshake and connection lifecycle
topics.summary: The TCP handshake and connection lifecycle establish reliable ordered byte streams, then tear them down with FIN or RST behavior. Connection setup, reuse, idle timeouts, and keepalives affect latency and failure handling.

topics.title: TCP congestion and packet loss
topics.summary: TCP congestion control adjusts sending rate based on acknowledgements, loss, delay, and congestion window behavior. Packet loss and retransmits can turn a healthy service into a slow one before application metrics show errors.

topics.title: UDP, QUIC, and connection migration
topics.summary: UDP gives applications datagrams without TCP's built-in reliability, while QUIC builds encrypted streams, loss recovery, and connection migration over UDP. This changes how latency, packet loss, and client network changes are handled.

topics.title: MTU, fragmentation, and PMTUD
topics.summary: MTU limits the largest packet a path can carry without fragmentation. Path MTU discovery failures can produce confusing partial outages where small requests work and larger responses stall.

topics.title: Load balancer algorithms
topics.summary: Load balancer algorithms choose targets with policies such as round robin, least connections, weighted routing, hashing, locality, or latency. The choice affects fairness, cache locality, stickiness, failure recovery, and hot spots.

groups.name: Security and access control
groups.note: Use this group to make network access explicit through firewalls, private links, zero-trust policy, and traffic protection.

topics.title: Firewall rule ordering
topics.summary: Firewall rule ordering determines which allow or deny rule applies first. Specificity, default deny, explicit egress, logging, and rule shadowing are essential for both security and debugging.

topics.title: Security groups vs network ACLs
topics.summary: Security groups and network ACLs apply network policy at different scopes and with different state behavior. Engineers should understand instance, subnet, stateful, stateless, inbound, and outbound rule implications.

topics.title: VPN and private connectivity
topics.summary: VPN and private connectivity link users, offices, clouds, and partners without exposing services publicly. Designs must cover routing, authentication, split tunnel behavior, overlapping CIDRs, failover, and auditability.

topics.title: Zero trust network access
topics.summary: Zero trust network access grants service access based on identity, device posture, context, and policy rather than broad network location. It shrinks implicit trust but requires strong identity, logging, and exception handling.

topics.title: DDoS protection and traffic scrubbing
topics.summary: DDoS protection and traffic scrubbing absorb or filter malicious floods before they exhaust application, network, or origin capacity. Useful defenses combine edge capacity, rate limits, challenge flows, filtering, and runbooks.

groups.name: Service networking and cloud topology
groups.note: Use this group to design how services, VPCs, gateways, regions, discovery, and address families connect.

topics.title: VPC peering and transit gateways
topics.summary: VPC peering and transit gateways connect private networks with different scaling and routing properties. Topology choices affect blast radius, route propagation, inspection points, and ownership boundaries.

topics.title: Service discovery and DNS-based routing
topics.summary: Service discovery lets callers find healthy service instances or stable service names. DNS-based discovery is simple and portable, but TTLs, negative caching, health checks, and client caching shape failover behavior.

topics.title: Ingress and egress gateway design
topics.summary: Ingress and egress gateways centralize traffic entry and exit for policy, observability, routing, and security controls. They also become critical-path infrastructure with capacity and failure-mode obligations.

topics.title: Multi-region failover routing
topics.summary: Multi-region failover routing directs users away from unhealthy regions while balancing recovery time, data consistency, DNS or edge cache behavior, and traffic-drain safety. It must be tested before an incident.

topics.title: IPv4 vs IPv6 dual-stack
topics.summary: IPv4 and IPv6 dual-stack systems support both address families across DNS, routing, firewalls, load balancers, clients, and observability. Partial dual-stack rollouts can produce asymmetric reachability failures.

groups.name: Observability and troubleshooting
groups.note: Use this group to diagnose network behavior with captures, traces, probes, SLOs, and incident triage routines.

topics.title: Packet capture fundamentals
topics.summary: Packet capture fundamentals help engineers inspect actual traffic rather than inferred application behavior. Good captures choose the right interface, filters, time window, and privacy boundaries.

topics.title: Traceroute and path diagnosis
topics.summary: Traceroute and path diagnosis reveal likely network hops, latency jumps, and routing asymmetry. Results require interpretation because rate limits, firewalls, tunnels, and ICMP policy can hide or distort hops.

topics.title: Synthetic network probes
topics.summary: Synthetic network probes continuously test reachability, DNS, TLS, latency, packet loss, and regional routing from controlled vantage points. They catch network-path problems before users or services report them.

topics.title: SLOs for network reliability
topics.summary: Network reliability SLOs define measurable expectations for availability, latency, loss, DNS success, TLS success, and regional reachability. They connect lower-level signals to user-visible service behavior.

topics.title: Incident triage for network partitions
topics.summary: Network partition triage separates application failure from reachability, DNS, routing, firewall, load balancer, or provider issues. Responders need a disciplined path from symptom to packet path to ownership.

roles.description: Foundational concepts a junior engineer should be able to recognize, explain, and apply with guidance.

roles.description: Concepts a mid-level engineer should be able to apply independently in routine product and platform work.

roles.description: Concepts a senior engineer should be able to use for design trade-offs, production debugging, and technical leadership.

roles.description: Concepts a staff-level engineer should be able to apply across teams, platform boundaries, and long-lived architecture decisions.

roles.description: Requirements for general software craft: modularity, domain modeling, contracts, testing, refactoring, debugging, code review, documentation, and maintainability.

roles.label: Design

roles.label: Design system

roles.label: System design

roles.label: Developer experience
roles.description: Requirements for tools, templates, generated artifacts, platform ergonomics, and paved paths that improve engineering workflows.

roles.label: Product
roles.description: Requirements that connect engineering concepts to product decisions, user impact, reporting, or business semantics.

topics.title: Pointer events
topics.summary: Pointer events unify mouse, touch, pen, and stylus input behind one event model. A strong explanation covers pointerId, pointerType, pressure, pointer capture, cancellation, and why duplicating mouse/touch logic creates gesture bugs.

topics.title: ARIA live regions internals
topics.summary: ARIA live regions are parts of the DOM that assistive technologies monitor for announcements. The important details are politeness level, atomic updates, insertion timing, and avoiding rapid DOM replacement that screen readers may ignore.

topics.title: Accessibility tree
topics.summary: The accessibility tree is the browser-derived semantic representation exposed to assistive technologies. It is built from DOM, native semantics, ARIA, CSS visibility, names, descriptions, focusability, and platform mappings.

topics.title: Idempotent UI actions
topics.summary: An idempotent UI action produces the same durable result even if the user clicks twice, the request retries, or the component remounts. The usual tools are action keys, disabled states, dedupe maps, idempotency headers, and server-side replay protection.

topics.title: Deterministic rendering
topics.summary: Deterministic rendering means the same inputs produce the same UI output. It avoids hidden time, random values, mutable globals, request order dependence, and client/server mismatches during hydration.

topics.title: Priority inversion in async code
topics.summary: Priority inversion happens when urgent work waits behind lower-priority work because the scheduler or promise chain cannot preempt it. In UI this shows up as input blocked behind rendering, background fetches, or heavy microtask chains.

topics.title: Speculative prerendering
topics.summary: Speculative prerendering asks the browser to prepare likely future navigations before the user clicks. It can make navigations instant, but must avoid private-state leaks, side effects, wasted bandwidth, and analytics double-counting.

topics.title: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
topics.summary: LCP measures when the largest visible content element in the viewport is rendered. Good explanations connect LCP to TTFB, render-blocking CSS, image discovery, resource priority, server rendering, and client-side render delays.

topics.title: Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
topics.summary: CLS measures unexpected visual movement during page lifetime. The core prevention model is reserving space, stable dimensions, predictable font loading, non-intrusive ads/embeds, and avoiding DOM insertions above existing content.

topics.title: Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
topics.summary: INP measures the latency of user interactions from input through processing to the next paint. It rewards short event handlers, quick style/layout work, cooperative yielding, and avoiding long main-thread tasks.

topics.title: First Input Delay (FID)
topics.summary: FID measured the delay before the browser could start processing the first input. It is largely a main-thread availability metric and is best explained historically as the predecessor to INP for interaction responsiveness.

topics.title: Long tasks API
topics.summary: The Long Tasks API exposes main-thread tasks that run long enough to block input and rendering. It is useful for finding expensive scripts, hydration bursts, synchronous parsing, and third-party code that creates responsiveness cliffs.

topics.title: PerformanceObserver API
topics.summary: PerformanceObserver streams browser or runtime performance entries as they occur, often with buffered historical entries. It is the common mechanism for collecting vitals, resource timing, long tasks, marks, and measures.

topics.title: Garbage collection timing
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Garbage collection is nondeterministic and should not be part of application correctness. A frontend engineer should understand object reachability, closures, event listeners, WeakMap/WeakRef trade-offs, and why GC pauses can affect responsiveness.

topics.title: Detached DOM nodes
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Detached DOM nodes are removed from the visible document but still retained by JavaScript references. They often come from leaked listeners, caches, closures, observers, and component cleanup bugs.

topics.title: Browser memory leak detection
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Browser memory leak detection is the process of proving memory grows because objects remain reachable after expected cleanup. Good explanations include heap snapshots, allocation timelines, detached DOM node views, listener cleanup, and reproducible interaction loops.

topics.title: Streaming fetch response handling
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Streaming fetch handling reads response chunks as they arrive instead of waiting for the full body. It enables progressive rendering, lower memory usage, server-sent protocols, and earlier cancellation.

topics.title: AbortController
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: AbortController coordinates cancellation for fetches, streams, event listeners, and async operations. It prevents stale updates, leaked work, unnecessary network traffic, and component-unmount races.

topics.title: Backpressure in streams API
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Backpressure is the signal that a consumer cannot keep up with a producer. Streams expose it through desiredSize, writer.ready, highWaterMark, drain-like behavior, and async pulls to avoid unbounded buffering.

topics.title: WebRTC
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: WebRTC provides peer-to-peer media and data channels with NAT traversal, ICE, STUN/TURN, SDP negotiation, encryption, congestion control, and real-time delivery constraints.

topics.title: CRDT basics for collaboration
topics.summary: CRDTs are data types designed so replicas can update independently and merge without conflicts. A clear answer covers commutativity, associativity, idempotent merges, causal metadata, and trade-offs in metadata size.

topics.title: Offline conflict resolution
topics.summary: Offline conflict resolution decides what happens when local changes meet remote changes after reconnect. Strategies include last-write-wins, field-level merge, operational transforms, CRDTs, manual conflict UI, and version vectors.

topics.title: Optimistic UI rollback strategy
topics.summary: Optimistic UI applies a predicted result immediately, then confirms or rolls back after the server responds. A reliable strategy records previous state, pending operation IDs, failure rules, and reconciliation with server truth.

topics.title: Event sourcing in frontend
topics.summary: Frontend event sourcing stores user/domain events and derives UI state from projections. It helps with undo/redo, offline queues, auditability, replay, optimistic updates, and deterministic debugging.

topics.title: Finite state modeling
topics.summary: Finite state modeling describes UI behavior as explicit states and allowed transitions. It prevents impossible states like loading and saved simultaneously, and makes retries, errors, and cancellation easier to test.

topics.title: Micro-frontend orchestration
topics.summary: Micro-frontend orchestration coordinates independently built frontend applications at runtime. Strong explanations cover ownership boundaries, routing, shared dependencies, CSS isolation, versioning, event contracts, and failure containment.

topics.title: Edge rendering
topics.summary: Edge rendering produces HTML or responses close to users, usually in geographically distributed runtimes. It improves latency but constrains APIs, cold starts, data locality, cache behavior, and consistency.

topics.title: Server components
topics.summary: Server components render parts of the component tree on the server without shipping their implementation to the client. The core trade-off is reduced client JavaScript versus stricter serialization, data access, and boundary rules.

topics.title: Selective hydration
topics.summary: Selective hydration hydrates only the interactive parts of server-rendered HTML, often by priority or visibility. It reduces startup work, but requires accurate island boundaries and safe event replay or delayed interactivity.

topics.title: Suspense boundaries
topics.summary: Suspense boundaries isolate async waiting so one slow dependency does not block the entire UI. A strong explanation mentions fallback UI, reveal order, thrown promises/resource reads, streaming SSR, and avoiding waterfalls.

topics.title: Render waterfalls
topics.summary: Render waterfalls happen when rendering discovers async dependencies sequentially instead of in parallel. They commonly occur in nested components, route loaders, dynamic imports, and suspense trees that fetch too late.

topics.title: Scheduler priorities
topics.summary: Scheduler priorities decide which work should run now and which work can wait. UI schedulers prioritize input and visible updates over background rendering, prefetching, analytics, and non-urgent transitions.

topics.title: Tearing in concurrent UI
topics.summary: Tearing occurs when different parts of the UI observe different versions of shared state during concurrent rendering. Avoid it with consistent snapshots, subscription protocols, immutable commits, and framework-specific external-store APIs.

topics.title: Race conditions in UI state
topics.summary: UI state races happen when async results arrive out of order or after the state they depended on has changed. Common fixes are request IDs, AbortController, version checks, state machines, and idempotent reducers.

topics.title: Prototype pollution
topics.summary: Prototype pollution lets attacker-controlled keys modify Object.prototype or constructors. It often comes from unsafe deep merge, path setters, query parsers, or JSON merge logic that accepts __proto__, prototype, or constructor keys.

topics.title: DOM clobbering
topics.summary: DOM clobbering abuses named elements or IDs that become properties on document, forms, or windows. Safe code avoids trusting global property lookup and reads explicit attributes from selected elements instead.

topics.title: Trusted Types
topics.summary: Trusted Types is a browser defense that restricts dangerous DOM sinks such as innerHTML to values created by approved policies. It is especially useful for reducing DOM XSS in large applications.

topics.title: Content Security Policy (CSP)
topics.summary: CSP is a browser-enforced policy controlling where scripts, styles, images, frames, and other resources can load from. Strong explanations cover nonces, hashes, strict-dynamic, report-only rollout, and blocking inline script execution.

topics.title: CSRF vs XSS mitigation
topics.summary: CSRF tricks an authenticated browser into sending unwanted state-changing requests; XSS executes attacker script in the trusted origin. CSRF is mitigated with SameSite, tokens, and origin checks; XSS is mitigated with output encoding, CSP, sanitization, and Trusted Types.

topics.title: SameSite cookie modes
topics.summary: SameSite controls whether cookies are sent on cross-site requests. Lax is a pragmatic default, Strict is more protective but can break flows, and None requires Secure for third-party contexts.

topics.title: CORS preflight
topics.summary: A CORS preflight is an OPTIONS request the browser sends before non-simple cross-origin requests. The server must explicitly allow origin, methods, and headers; CORS is a browser boundary, not server-to-server auth.

topics.title: Preload vs Prefetch vs Preconnect
topics.summary: Preload fetches a needed resource for the current navigation, prefetch gets likely future resources at lower priority, and preconnect warms DNS/TCP/TLS connections to an origin. Misuse can waste bandwidth or hurt priority scheduling.

topics.title: Priority hints
topics.summary: Priority hints communicate relative fetch importance to the browser. They are useful for hero images and noncritical assets, but should complement rather than replace correct resource discovery and markup order.

topics.title: HTTP/3 and QUIC
topics.summary: HTTP/3 runs HTTP semantics over QUIC instead of TCP. It reduces transport head-of-line blocking, integrates TLS 1.3, supports connection migration, and handles loss recovery per stream more gracefully than HTTP/2 over TCP.

topics.title: ETag vs Cache-Control
topics.summary: Cache-Control defines freshness and reuse rules; ETag is a validator for conditional revalidation. Effective caching uses both: freshness for fast reuse and validators for cheap correctness after stale entries.

topics.title: Stale-while-revalidate
topics.summary: Stale-while-revalidate serves a cached stale response immediately while refreshing in the background. It improves perceived latency but requires tolerance for temporary staleness and careful invalidation for user-specific data.

topics.title: Cache invalidation strategies
topics.summary: Cache invalidation is the policy for removing or superseding cached data when truth changes. Techniques include TTLs, versioned keys, surrogate keys, write-through updates, event-driven purges, and scoped cache busting.

topics.title: Service Worker lifecycle traps
topics.summary: Service Workers have install, waiting, activate, fetch, and update states that can keep old code alive. Traps include stale caches, uncontrolled clients, skipWaiting misuse, update races, and broken offline fallbacks.

topics.title: IndexedDB
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: IndexedDB is the browser's transactional object store for larger structured data. Good explanations mention version upgrades, object stores, indexes, transactions, async request APIs, quota, and offline-first storage.

topics.title: MutationObserver cost
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: MutationObserver batches DOM mutation records, but broad subtree observation can be expensive. The cost comes from record volume, callback work, retained nodes, and accidental feedback loops that create more mutations.

topics.title: ResizeObserver loop limits
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: ResizeObserver reports element size changes, but writing size-affecting styles inside the callback can create loops. Browsers limit these loops, so callbacks should defer writes and avoid recursive layout changes.

topics.title: IntersectionObserver internals
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: IntersectionObserver asynchronously reports visibility intersections between targets and a root. It avoids many scroll-handler costs, but callbacks are still approximate, threshold-based, and affected by root margins and layout changes.

topics.title: Subpixel rendering
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: Subpixel rendering occurs because layout uses fractional CSS pixels while screens use device pixels. Rounding can affect text, transforms, borders, canvas drawing, and alignment across devicePixelRatio values.

topics.title: CSS containment
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: CSS containment tells the browser that layout, paint, style, or size effects are isolated. It lets the engine skip broader invalidation and is especially useful for virtualized lists, cards, and independent widgets.

topics.title: GPU acceleration in CSS
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: GPU acceleration usually means moving compositable work such as transforms and opacity to compositor layers. It can improve animation smoothness but too many layers waste memory and can hurt performance.

topics.title: Paint vs composite vs layout
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: Layout computes geometry, paint rasterizes pixels, and composite assembles layers on screen. Performance work often means avoiding layout and paint when a transform or opacity-only composite will do.

topics.title: Browser compositing layers
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: Compositing layers are independently rasterized surfaces the compositor can move or blend. They are created by transforms, opacity, video, fixed elements, will-change, and browser heuristics, but each layer has memory and upload cost.

topics.title: WebAssembly integration
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: WebAssembly integration loads compiled modules into JavaScript for CPU-heavy, portable code. The real boundary is memory copying, async instantiation, imports/exports, streaming compilation, and choosing where JS remains simpler.

topics.title: OffscreenCanvas
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: OffscreenCanvas allows canvas rendering off the main thread, often in a Worker. It is useful for charts, games, image processing, and avoiding main-thread paint pressure.

topics.title: Transferable objects
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Transferable objects move ownership of buffers or ports between threads without copying. After transfer, the original owner is detached, which improves performance but requires explicit lifetime handling.

topics.title: SharedArrayBuffer
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: SharedArrayBuffer allows multiple threads to access the same memory with Atomics for coordination. In browsers it requires cross-origin isolation because of side-channel risk.

topics.title: Web Workers vs Service Workers
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Web Workers run background JavaScript for a page; Service Workers act as network/proxy lifecycle scripts for an origin scope. Workers help CPU isolation, while Service Workers intercept requests, cache, and enable offline behavior.

topics.title: Web Components interoperability
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Web Components interoperate through custom elements, attributes, properties, events, slots, and DOM APIs. Good boundaries avoid framework-specific assumptions and expose stable platform contracts.

topics.title: Custom Elements lifecycle
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Custom Elements lifecycle callbacks handle construction, connection, disconnection, adoption, and observed attribute changes. Correct components defer DOM work until connected and clean up listeners, observers, and async work on disconnect.

topics.title: Shadow DOM
topics.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
topics.summary: Shadow DOM creates an encapsulated DOM subtree with scoped styling and slot-based composition. It improves component isolation but affects styling, event retargeting, accessibility names, and testing strategies.

topics.title: Module federation
topics.summary: Module federation loads code from independently deployed builds at runtime. It enables separate ownership and deployment but introduces version negotiation, shared dependency, fallback, security, and observability problems.

topics.title: Dynamic import chunking
topics.summary: Dynamic import creates async module boundaries that bundlers can split into separate chunks. It is useful for route-level, feature-level, and conditionally loaded code, but too many chunks create network overhead.

topics.title: Code splitting strategies
topics.summary: Code splitting decides which code ships together and which code loads later. Useful strategies include route splitting, component splitting, vendor splitting, permission-based loading, and interaction-triggered loading.

topics.title: Tree shaking internals
topics.summary: Tree shaking removes unused exports by static analysis of ESM imports/exports. It works best with side-effect-free modules, direct imports, and package sideEffects metadata.

topics.title: Render blocking resources
topics.summary: Render-blocking resources delay first paint or meaningful rendering because the browser must fetch, parse, or execute them first. CSS, synchronous scripts, fonts, and late-discovered hero assets are common causes.

topics.title: Critical rendering path
topics.summary: The critical rendering path is the sequence from HTML bytes to DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, and composite. Optimizing it means reducing blocking resources and making important content discoverable early.

topics.title: Layout thrashing
topics.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
topics.summary: Layout thrashing alternates DOM reads that force layout with writes that invalidate layout. Batch reads before writes, use transforms for motion, and avoid measuring after each mutation.

topics.title: Task starvation
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Task starvation happens when one class of work keeps the event loop from processing another. Infinite microtask chains, heavy sync loops, or too many high-priority tasks can starve input, timers, rendering, or I/O.

topics.title: Event loop (macro vs microtasks)
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: The event loop runs synchronous code, then microtasks, then macrotasks and rendering opportunities. Promises and queueMicrotask run before timers, which can be good for consistency but dangerous when chains are unbounded.

topics.title: Stale closure problem
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: A stale closure uses values captured from an earlier render or state version. It appears in handlers, timers, promises, subscriptions, and memoized callbacks that outlive the data they closed over.

topics.title: Memoization pitfalls
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Memoization can hide expensive work, but wrong keys, mutable inputs, unbounded caches, and referential churn can make it incorrect or slower. It is a trade-off between CPU, memory, invalidation, and complexity.

topics.title: Referential equality
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Referential equality compares object identity rather than deep value. UI frameworks use it for memoization and update detection, so recreating objects or functions can trigger unnecessary work.

topics.title: Immutable data patterns
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Immutable data patterns create new values instead of mutating existing state. They make change detection, undo, time travel, concurrency, and structural sharing easier.

topics.title: Structural sharing
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Structural sharing reuses unchanged parts of immutable data structures. It reduces memory churn and lets referential equality identify which subtrees changed.

topics.title: Virtual DOM diffing complexity
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Virtual DOM diffing compares previous and next trees to compute DOM operations. Keys reduce expensive ambiguity in lists, while unstable keys or deep tree churn increase work and bugs.

topics.title: Fiber architecture
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Fiber architecture breaks rendering work into interruptible units. It enables prioritization, pausing, resuming, aborting, and committing work separately from rendering calculations.

topics.title: Reconciliation algorithm
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Reconciliation decides how a framework maps a new UI description onto existing component or DOM instances. Keyed identity, component type, position, and state preservation rules are central.

topics.title: Time slicing
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Time slicing breaks long rendering or computation into chunks so the event loop can process input and paint. It improves responsiveness but requires work to be restartable and side effects to be delayed.

topics.title: Concurrent rendering
topics.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
topics.summary: Concurrent rendering lets a framework prepare new UI without immediately committing it. It enables interruptible rendering and prioritization, but requires avoiding side effects during render and preventing tearing.

topics.title: Streaming SSR
topics.summary: Streaming SSR sends HTML progressively while data or components are still resolving. It improves time to first byte and progressive display, but requires boundary management, script ordering, and hydration coordination.

topics.title: Islands architecture
topics.summary: Islands architecture renders mostly static HTML and hydrates isolated interactive components. It reduces client JavaScript and hydration cost, but boundaries and cross-island communication must be explicit.

topics.title: Partial hydration
topics.summary: Partial hydration hydrates only parts of a server-rendered page rather than the full tree. It is related to islands and resumability, and trades framework complexity for less startup JavaScript.

topics.title: Hydration
topics.summary: Hydration attaches client behavior to server-rendered HTML. The hard parts are matching server/client output, event replay, async data consistency, and avoiding large startup work.

topics.title: Cohesion and coupling
topics.summary: Cohesion measures how strongly the responsibilities inside a module belong together, while coupling measures how much that module depends on other modules. Good software engineering raises cohesion and controls coupling so changes stay local.

topics.title: Abstraction boundaries
topics.summary: An abstraction boundary exposes what callers need while hiding volatile implementation details. The boundary should make correct use easier, make invalid use harder, and leave room for implementation changes.

topics.title: Information hiding
topics.summary: Information hiding keeps decisions that are likely to change inside one module instead of leaking them into every caller. It protects code from ripple effects when storage, parsing, algorithms, or vendor behavior changes.

topics.title: Dependency direction
topics.summary: Dependency direction decides which modules know about which other modules. Stable business rules should not depend on volatile delivery details such as HTTP, CLIs, files, framework adapters, or UI shells.

topics.title: Composition over inheritance
topics.summary: Composition builds behavior by passing collaborators or functions together, while inheritance shares behavior through parent classes. Composition usually makes behavior easier to test, replace, and combine without deep class hierarchies.

topics.title: Domain modeling
topics.summary: Domain modeling captures the names, rules, states, and workflows of the problem space in code. Strong models reduce translation errors between product language, data structures, and business behavior.

topics.title: Invariants
topics.summary: Invariants are facts that must remain true before and after operations. Naming invariants explicitly turns hidden assumptions into validations, tests, constructors, and state transition rules.

topics.title: Value objects
topics.summary: Value objects represent values by their contents instead of identity. They are useful for money, email addresses, quantities, ranges, and other concepts that need validation and equality semantics.

topics.title: Error handling strategy
topics.summary: Error handling strategy decides which failures throw, which return typed outcomes, which retry, which are user-visible, and which are programmer bugs. A consistent strategy keeps failures inspectable instead of accidental.

topics.title: Result types and explicit outcomes
topics.summary: Result types represent success and failure as data. They are useful when callers are expected to branch on known outcomes such as validation failures, missing records, authorization decisions, or conflicts.

topics.title: API contracts inside a codebase
topics.summary: Internal APIs still need contracts: inputs, outputs, side effects, errors, ordering, idempotency, and compatibility expectations. Clear internal contracts reduce coordination cost between modules and teams.

topics.title: Backward-compatible change
topics.summary: Backward-compatible change lets existing callers continue working while new behavior rolls out. Practical compatibility includes additive fields, tolerant readers, deprecation windows, feature flags, and migration helpers.

topics.title: Unit test boundaries
topics.summary: Unit tests should focus on meaningful behavior at a stable boundary, not private implementation trivia. Good unit boundaries make fast tests valuable while leaving room to refactor internals.

topics.title: Integration test boundaries
topics.summary: Integration tests verify that real collaborators work together across module, process, storage, or protocol boundaries. They should cover risky contracts that unit tests cannot prove.

topics.title: Test doubles
topics.summary: Test doubles replace real collaborators with fakes, stubs, spies, or mocks. They are useful when the double preserves the contract being tested, but harmful when they only mirror implementation details.

topics.title: Property-based testing
topics.summary: Property-based testing checks general rules across many generated inputs instead of only named examples. It is useful for parsers, formatters, reducers, validators, and algorithms with durable invariants.

topics.title: Mutation testing
topics.summary: Mutation testing changes code in small ways and checks whether tests fail. Surviving mutations show where tests execute code without proving the behavior that matters.

topics.title: Refactoring in small steps
topics.summary: Refactoring changes code structure without changing observable behavior. Small verified steps reduce risk by keeping each move understandable, reversible, and covered by existing or characterization tests.

topics.title: Code smells
topics.summary: Code smells are signals that code may be harder to change than necessary. Long functions, shotgun changes, primitive obsession, feature envy, and duplicate logic are prompts to investigate, not automatic verdicts.

topics.title: Technical debt management
topics.summary: Technical debt is a design or implementation trade-off that creates future carrying cost. Good debt management names the cost, owner, trigger for repayment, and risk if it remains unpaid.

topics.title: Legacy code characterization
topics.summary: Characterization tests capture what legacy code currently does before changing it. They create a safety net when requirements are unclear, behavior is surprising, or refactoring must preserve quirks.

topics.title: Feature toggle cleanup
topics.summary: Feature toggles should have owners, expiry dates, and cleanup plans. Stale toggles create hidden branches, test matrix growth, configuration risk, and dead code.

topics.title: Code review quality
topics.summary: Code review quality depends on reviewing behavior, risk, maintainability, tests, naming, compatibility, and operational impact. Reviews should make the change better without becoming a style-only gate.

topics.title: Architecture decision records
topics.summary: Architecture decision records capture the context, options, decision, and consequences of important technical choices. They help future engineers understand why a design exists before changing it.

topics.title: Estimation and risk slicing
topics.summary: Estimation improves when work is sliced around uncertainty, dependencies, feedback, and irreversible decisions. Risk-first slices turn unknowns into evidence before committing to a large implementation path.

topics.title: Documentation close to code
topics.summary: Documentation close to code keeps examples, contracts, commands, and design notes near the implementation they describe. It reduces drift when docs can be reviewed and regenerated with code changes.

topics.title: Systematic debugging
topics.summary: Systematic debugging forms a hypothesis, chooses the smallest useful observation, compares expected and actual behavior, and updates the model. It prevents random edits from hiding the real cause.

topics.title: Contextual logging
topics.summary: Contextual logging records enough stable identifiers and state to reconstruct behavior without dumping sensitive data. Good logs explain what happened, where, for whom, and why the code chose that path.

topics.title: Configuration boundaries
topics.summary: Configuration boundaries separate code from environment-specific values while keeping validation close to startup. Strong config boundaries prevent missing, misspelled, or incompatible settings from failing deep in runtime.

topics.title: Performance profiling before optimization
topics.summary: Performance profiling measures where time, memory, or I/O is actually spent before changing code. Profiling protects teams from optimizing the wrong path or trading clarity for unmeasured speed.

topics.title: Design system purpose and governance
topics.summary: A design system is the operating layer between product design, UI engineering, and shipped interfaces. Governance defines who can change tokens, components, Figma libraries, package APIs, documentation, and release policy.

topics.title: Component inventory and audit
topics.summary: A component inventory identifies repeated UI patterns, implementation variants, usage frequency, accessibility risk, and ownership gaps. It turns vague design debt into a prioritized system backlog.

topics.title: Design language taxonomy
topics.summary: Design language taxonomy names the primitives, patterns, templates, and product-specific exceptions in a shared vocabulary. Clear taxonomy keeps Figma names, component names, token names, and documentation aligned.

topics.title: Accessibility as a design constraint
topics.summary: Accessibility belongs in design decisions before implementation. Color contrast, focus order, target size, motion, labels, keyboard behavior, and error messaging should be treated as design constraints, not late QA fixes.

topics.title: Contribution model and ownership
topics.summary: A contribution model explains how teams propose, review, build, document, and release system changes. It defines ownership across design, engineering, accessibility, product, and platform maintainers.

topics.title: Design token architecture
topics.summary: Design token architecture separates raw values, semantic decisions, component aliases, and platform outputs. This lets a color, spacing, typography, or motion decision move from design source to code without hardcoded drift.

topics.title: Token naming and semantic layers
topics.summary: Token names should encode intent rather than current visual appearance. Semantic layers such as surface, text, border, action, and feedback survive rebrands better than names like blue-500 or gray-light.

topics.title: Figma variables to code tokens
topics.summary: Figma variables become reliable code tokens only when naming, modes, aliases, exports, review, and versioning are explicit. The pipeline should detect missing mappings before app code consumes broken values.

topics.title: Theme modes and brand theming
topics.summary: Theme modes map the same semantic token names to different values for light, dark, high-contrast, brand, or tenant contexts. The component API should consume stable semantics, not mode-specific literals.

topics.title: Token versioning and migration
topics.summary: Token versioning protects consuming apps when a token is renamed, removed, or changes meaning. Migration notes, aliases, deprecation windows, and codemods keep design changes from becoming scattered UI regressions.

topics.title: Figma component variants
topics.summary: Figma variants model the supported visual states and options for a component. They should map closely to code props so designers and engineers are discussing the same combinations and constraints.

topics.title: Auto layout and responsive constraints
topics.summary: Auto layout and responsive constraints make design intent explicit for spacing, wrapping, alignment, truncation, and resizing. They reduce ambiguity when a Figma frame becomes real CSS layout.

topics.title: Design spec handoff quality
topics.summary: Design handoff quality depends on states, content rules, accessibility notes, responsive behavior, data edge cases, and interaction timing. A polished static frame is not enough to implement durable UI.

topics.title: GitHub issues for design changes
topics.summary: GitHub issues connect design requests to engineering review, implementation, tests, release notes, and linked Figma evidence. They make design system changes traceable instead of scattered across comments and chat.

topics.title: Design review acceptance criteria
topics.summary: Design review acceptance criteria define what must be true before a component change ships: visual match, accessible behavior, documented states, responsive behavior, analytics impact, and migration guidance.

topics.title: Component prop API design
topics.summary: Component prop APIs translate design intent into reusable engineering interfaces. Good APIs expose stable semantic choices, prevent invalid combinations, and leave room for content and accessibility requirements.

topics.title: Slots composition and escape hatches
topics.summary: Slots and composition let product teams place custom content inside system components without forking them. Escape hatches should be deliberate, documented, and constrained so they do not undermine consistency.

topics.title: Controlled vs uncontrolled components
topics.summary: Controlled components let app state own the value, while uncontrolled components keep internal state until a boundary event. Design system components should choose the model that matches validation, form, and composition needs.

topics.title: Visual states and interaction contracts
topics.summary: Visual states such as hover, focus, disabled, loading, selected, invalid, and pressed are interaction contracts. They should be represented in design, documentation, tests, and implementation with the same names.

topics.title: Styling strategy for component libraries
topics.summary: A component library styling strategy decides how tokens, CSS variables, cascade layers, class names, composition, and app overrides interact. The strategy should protect consistency while allowing product-specific layout.

topics.title: Storybook-driven documentation
topics.summary: Storybook-style documentation pairs component examples with props, states, accessibility notes, tokens, and usage guidance. It becomes a shared review surface for design, engineering, QA, and product teams.

topics.title: Visual regression testing
topics.summary: Visual regression testing compares rendered component states across changes to catch unintended appearance shifts. It is most useful when snapshots represent real supported states instead of random page screenshots.

topics.title: Interaction and accessibility tests
topics.summary: Interaction and accessibility tests verify keyboard flow, focus management, ARIA state, labels, disabled behavior, and event timing. They protect behavior that visual review alone cannot reliably catch.

topics.title: Changelog and release notes for components
