nodes.label: SameSite cookie modes
nodes.summary: SameSite controls whether cookies are sent on cross-site requests. Lax is a pragmatic default, Strict is more protective but can break flows, and None requires Secure for third-party contexts.

nodes.label: CORS preflight
nodes.summary: A CORS preflight is an OPTIONS request the browser sends before non-simple cross-origin requests. The server must explicitly allow origin, methods, and headers; CORS is a browser boundary, not server-to-server auth.

nodes.label: Preload vs Prefetch vs Preconnect
nodes.summary: Preload fetches a needed resource for the current navigation, prefetch gets likely future resources at lower priority, and preconnect warms DNS/TCP/TLS connections to an origin. Misuse can waste bandwidth or hurt priority scheduling.

nodes.label: Priority hints
nodes.summary: Priority hints communicate relative fetch importance to the browser. They are useful for hero images and noncritical assets, but should complement rather than replace correct resource discovery and markup order.

nodes.label: HTTP/3 and QUIC
nodes.summary: HTTP/3 runs HTTP semantics over QUIC instead of TCP. It reduces transport head-of-line blocking, integrates TLS 1.3, supports connection migration, and handles loss recovery per stream more gracefully than HTTP/2 over TCP.

nodes.label: ETag vs Cache-Control
nodes.summary: Cache-Control defines freshness and reuse rules; ETag is a validator for conditional revalidation. Effective caching uses both: freshness for fast reuse and validators for cheap correctness after stale entries.

nodes.label: Stale-while-revalidate
nodes.summary: Stale-while-revalidate serves a cached stale response immediately while refreshing in the background. It improves perceived latency but requires tolerance for temporary staleness and careful invalidation for user-specific data.

nodes.label: Cache invalidation strategies
nodes.summary: Cache invalidation is the policy for removing or superseding cached data when truth changes. Techniques include TTLs, versioned keys, surrogate keys, write-through updates, event-driven purges, and scoped cache busting.

nodes.label: Service Worker lifecycle traps
nodes.summary: Service Workers have install, waiting, activate, fetch, and update states that can keep old code alive. Traps include stale caches, uncontrolled clients, skipWaiting misuse, update races, and broken offline fallbacks.

nodes.label: IndexedDB
nodes.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
nodes.summary: IndexedDB is the browser's transactional object store for larger structured data. Good explanations mention version upgrades, object stores, indexes, transactions, async request APIs, quota, and offline-first storage.

nodes.label: MutationObserver cost
nodes.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
nodes.summary: MutationObserver batches DOM mutation records, but broad subtree observation can be expensive. The cost comes from record volume, callback work, retained nodes, and accidental feedback loops that create more mutations.

nodes.label: ResizeObserver loop limits
nodes.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
nodes.summary: ResizeObserver reports element size changes, but writing size-affecting styles inside the callback can create loops. Browsers limit these loops, so callbacks should defer writes and avoid recursive layout changes.

nodes.label: IntersectionObserver internals
nodes.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
nodes.summary: IntersectionObserver asynchronously reports visibility intersections between targets and a root. It avoids many scroll-handler costs, but callbacks are still approximate, threshold-based, and affected by root margins and layout changes.

nodes.label: Subpixel rendering
nodes.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
nodes.summary: Subpixel rendering occurs because layout uses fractional CSS pixels while screens use device pixels. Rounding can affect text, transforms, borders, canvas drawing, and alignment across devicePixelRatio values.

nodes.label: CSS containment
nodes.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
nodes.summary: CSS containment tells the browser that layout, paint, style, or size effects are isolated. It lets the engine skip broader invalidation and is especially useful for virtualized lists, cards, and independent widgets.

nodes.label: GPU acceleration in CSS
nodes.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
nodes.summary: GPU acceleration usually means moving compositable work such as transforms and opacity to compositor layers. It can improve animation smoothness but too many layers waste memory and can hurt performance.

nodes.label: Paint vs composite vs layout
nodes.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
nodes.summary: Layout computes geometry, paint rasterizes pixels, and composite assembles layers on screen. Performance work often means avoiding layout and paint when a transform or opacity-only composite will do.

nodes.label: Browser compositing layers
nodes.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
nodes.summary: Compositing layers are independently rasterized surfaces the compositor can move or blend. They are created by transforms, opacity, video, fixed elements, will-change, and browser heuristics, but each layer has memory and upload cost.

nodes.label: WebAssembly integration
nodes.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
nodes.summary: WebAssembly integration loads compiled modules into JavaScript for CPU-heavy, portable code. The real boundary is memory copying, async instantiation, imports/exports, streaming compilation, and choosing where JS remains simpler.

nodes.label: OffscreenCanvas
nodes.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
nodes.summary: OffscreenCanvas allows canvas rendering off the main thread, often in a Worker. It is useful for charts, games, image processing, and avoiding main-thread paint pressure.

nodes.label: Transferable objects
nodes.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
nodes.summary: Transferable objects move ownership of buffers or ports between threads without copying. After transfer, the original owner is detached, which improves performance but requires explicit lifetime handling.

nodes.label: SharedArrayBuffer
nodes.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
nodes.summary: SharedArrayBuffer allows multiple threads to access the same memory with Atomics for coordination. In browsers it requires cross-origin isolation because of side-channel risk.

nodes.label: Web Workers vs Service Workers
nodes.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
nodes.summary: Web Workers run background JavaScript for a page; Service Workers act as network/proxy lifecycle scripts for an origin scope. Workers help CPU isolation, while Service Workers intercept requests, cache, and enable offline behavior.

nodes.label: Web Components interoperability
nodes.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
nodes.summary: Web Components interoperate through custom elements, attributes, properties, events, slots, and DOM APIs. Good boundaries avoid framework-specific assumptions and expose stable platform contracts.

nodes.label: Custom Elements lifecycle
nodes.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
nodes.summary: Custom Elements lifecycle callbacks handle construction, connection, disconnection, adoption, and observed attribute changes. Correct components defer DOM work until connected and clean up listeners, observers, and async work on disconnect.

nodes.label: Shadow DOM
nodes.group: Memory, streams, and advanced browser APIs
nodes.summary: Shadow DOM creates an encapsulated DOM subtree with scoped styling and slot-based composition. It improves component isolation but affects styling, event retargeting, accessibility names, and testing strategies.

nodes.label: Module federation
nodes.summary: Module federation loads code from independently deployed builds at runtime. It enables separate ownership and deployment but introduces version negotiation, shared dependency, fallback, security, and observability problems.

nodes.label: Dynamic import chunking
nodes.summary: Dynamic import creates async module boundaries that bundlers can split into separate chunks. It is useful for route-level, feature-level, and conditionally loaded code, but too many chunks create network overhead.

nodes.label: Code splitting strategies
nodes.summary: Code splitting decides which code ships together and which code loads later. Useful strategies include route splitting, component splitting, vendor splitting, permission-based loading, and interaction-triggered loading.

nodes.label: Tree shaking internals
nodes.summary: Tree shaking removes unused exports by static analysis of ESM imports/exports. It works best with side-effect-free modules, direct imports, and package sideEffects metadata.

nodes.label: Render blocking resources
nodes.summary: Render-blocking resources delay first paint or meaningful rendering because the browser must fetch, parse, or execute them first. CSS, synchronous scripts, fonts, and late-discovered hero assets are common causes.

nodes.label: Critical rendering path
nodes.summary: The critical rendering path is the sequence from HTML bytes to DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, and composite. Optimizing it means reducing blocking resources and making important content discoverable early.

nodes.label: Layout thrashing
nodes.group: Observers, layout, paint, and CSS pipeline
nodes.summary: Layout thrashing alternates DOM reads that force layout with writes that invalidate layout. Batch reads before writes, use transforms for motion, and avoid measuring after each mutation.

nodes.label: Task starvation
nodes.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
nodes.summary: Task starvation happens when one class of work keeps the event loop from processing another. Infinite microtask chains, heavy sync loops, or too many high-priority tasks can starve input, timers, rendering, or I/O.

nodes.label: Event loop (macro vs microtasks)
nodes.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
nodes.summary: The event loop runs synchronous code, then microtasks, then macrotasks and rendering opportunities. Promises and queueMicrotask run before timers, which can be good for consistency but dangerous when chains are unbounded.

nodes.label: Stale closure problem
nodes.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
nodes.summary: A stale closure uses values captured from an earlier render or state version. It appears in handlers, timers, promises, subscriptions, and memoized callbacks that outlive the data they closed over.

nodes.label: Memoization pitfalls
nodes.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
nodes.summary: Memoization can hide expensive work, but wrong keys, mutable inputs, unbounded caches, and referential churn can make it incorrect or slower. It is a trade-off between CPU, memory, invalidation, and complexity.

nodes.label: Referential equality
nodes.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
nodes.summary: Referential equality compares object identity rather than deep value. UI frameworks use it for memoization and update detection, so recreating objects or functions can trigger unnecessary work.

nodes.label: Immutable data patterns
nodes.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
nodes.summary: Immutable data patterns create new values instead of mutating existing state. They make change detection, undo, time travel, concurrency, and structural sharing easier.

nodes.label: Structural sharing
nodes.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
nodes.summary: Structural sharing reuses unchanged parts of immutable data structures. It reduces memory churn and lets referential equality identify which subtrees changed.

nodes.label: Virtual DOM diffing complexity
nodes.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
nodes.summary: Virtual DOM diffing compares previous and next trees to compute DOM operations. Keys reduce expensive ambiguity in lists, while unstable keys or deep tree churn increase work and bugs.

nodes.label: Fiber architecture
nodes.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
nodes.summary: Fiber architecture breaks rendering work into interruptible units. It enables prioritization, pausing, resuming, aborting, and committing work separately from rendering calculations.

nodes.label: Reconciliation algorithm
nodes.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
nodes.summary: Reconciliation decides how a framework maps a new UI description onto existing component or DOM instances. Keyed identity, component type, position, and state preservation rules are central.

nodes.label: Time slicing
nodes.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
nodes.summary: Time slicing breaks long rendering or computation into chunks so the event loop can process input and paint. It improves responsiveness but requires work to be restartable and side effects to be delayed.

nodes.label: Concurrent rendering
nodes.group: Event loop, data identity, and UI algorithms
nodes.summary: Concurrent rendering lets a framework prepare new UI without immediately committing it. It enables interruptible rendering and prioritization, but requires avoiding side effects during render and preventing tearing.

nodes.label: Streaming SSR
nodes.summary: Streaming SSR sends HTML progressively while data or components are still resolving. It improves time to first byte and progressive display, but requires boundary management, script ordering, and hydration coordination.

nodes.label: Islands architecture
nodes.summary: Islands architecture renders mostly static HTML and hydrates isolated interactive components. It reduces client JavaScript and hydration cost, but boundaries and cross-island communication must be explicit.

nodes.label: Partial hydration
nodes.summary: Partial hydration hydrates only parts of a server-rendered page rather than the full tree. It is related to islands and resumability, and trades framework complexity for less startup JavaScript.

nodes.label: Hydration
nodes.summary: Hydration attaches client behavior to server-rendered HTML. The hard parts are matching server/client output, event replay, async data consistency, and avoiding large startup work.

nodes.label: Code structure and modularity
nodes.note: Use this group to reason about module shape, dependency direction, abstraction, information hiding, and how local code structure affects future change.

nodes.label: Modeling, APIs, and contracts
nodes.note: Use this group to express business rules, invariants, outcomes, and compatibility expectations directly in code boundaries.

nodes.label: Testing and quality signals
nodes.note: Use this group to choose tests that prove useful behavior instead of only executing implementation details.

nodes.label: Refactoring and evolution
nodes.note: Use this group to change code safely over time while managing debt, legacy behavior, toggles, and maintainability signals.

nodes.label: Collaboration and delivery discipline
nodes.note: Use this group to make software work reviewable, explainable, sliceable, and maintainable across a team.

nodes.label: Debugging, configuration, and runtime behavior
nodes.note: Use this group to connect everyday code decisions to diagnosis, configuration safety, logs, profiling, and production behavior.

nodes.label: Cohesion and coupling
nodes.summary: Cohesion measures how strongly the responsibilities inside a module belong together, while coupling measures how much that module depends on other modules. Good software engineering raises cohesion and controls coupling so changes stay local.

nodes.label: Abstraction boundaries
nodes.summary: An abstraction boundary exposes what callers need while hiding volatile implementation details. The boundary should make correct use easier, make invalid use harder, and leave room for implementation changes.

nodes.label: Information hiding
nodes.summary: Information hiding keeps decisions that are likely to change inside one module instead of leaking them into every caller. It protects code from ripple effects when storage, parsing, algorithms, or vendor behavior changes.

nodes.label: Dependency direction
nodes.summary: Dependency direction decides which modules know about which other modules. Stable business rules should not depend on volatile delivery details such as HTTP, CLIs, files, framework adapters, or UI shells.

nodes.label: Composition over inheritance
nodes.summary: Composition builds behavior by passing collaborators or functions together, while inheritance shares behavior through parent classes. Composition usually makes behavior easier to test, replace, and combine without deep class hierarchies.

nodes.label: Domain modeling
nodes.summary: Domain modeling captures the names, rules, states, and workflows of the problem space in code. Strong models reduce translation errors between product language, data structures, and business behavior.

nodes.label: Invariants
nodes.summary: Invariants are facts that must remain true before and after operations. Naming invariants explicitly turns hidden assumptions into validations, tests, constructors, and state transition rules.

nodes.label: Value objects
nodes.summary: Value objects represent values by their contents instead of identity. They are useful for money, email addresses, quantities, ranges, and other concepts that need validation and equality semantics.

nodes.label: Error handling strategy
nodes.summary: Error handling strategy decides which failures throw, which return typed outcomes, which retry, which are user-visible, and which are programmer bugs. A consistent strategy keeps failures inspectable instead of accidental.

nodes.label: Result types and explicit outcomes
nodes.summary: Result types represent success and failure as data. They are useful when callers are expected to branch on known outcomes such as validation failures, missing records, authorization decisions, or conflicts.

nodes.label: API contracts inside a codebase
nodes.summary: Internal APIs still need contracts: inputs, outputs, side effects, errors, ordering, idempotency, and compatibility expectations. Clear internal contracts reduce coordination cost between modules and teams.

nodes.label: Backward-compatible change
nodes.summary: Backward-compatible change lets existing callers continue working while new behavior rolls out. Practical compatibility includes additive fields, tolerant readers, deprecation windows, feature flags, and migration helpers.

nodes.label: Unit test boundaries
nodes.summary: Unit tests should focus on meaningful behavior at a stable boundary, not private implementation trivia. Good unit boundaries make fast tests valuable while leaving room to refactor internals.

nodes.label: Integration test boundaries
nodes.summary: Integration tests verify that real collaborators work together across module, process, storage, or protocol boundaries. They should cover risky contracts that unit tests cannot prove.

nodes.label: Test doubles
nodes.summary: Test doubles replace real collaborators with fakes, stubs, spies, or mocks. They are useful when the double preserves the contract being tested, but harmful when they only mirror implementation details.

nodes.label: Property-based testing
nodes.summary: Property-based testing checks general rules across many generated inputs instead of only named examples. It is useful for parsers, formatters, reducers, validators, and algorithms with durable invariants.

nodes.label: Mutation testing
nodes.summary: Mutation testing changes code in small ways and checks whether tests fail. Surviving mutations show where tests execute code without proving the behavior that matters.

nodes.label: Refactoring in small steps
nodes.summary: Refactoring changes code structure without changing observable behavior. Small verified steps reduce risk by keeping each move understandable, reversible, and covered by existing or characterization tests.

nodes.label: Code smells
nodes.summary: Code smells are signals that code may be harder to change than necessary. Long functions, shotgun changes, primitive obsession, feature envy, and duplicate logic are prompts to investigate, not automatic verdicts.

nodes.label: Technical debt management
nodes.summary: Technical debt is a design or implementation trade-off that creates future carrying cost. Good debt management names the cost, owner, trigger for repayment, and risk if it remains unpaid.

nodes.label: Legacy code characterization
nodes.summary: Characterization tests capture what legacy code currently does before changing it. They create a safety net when requirements are unclear, behavior is surprising, or refactoring must preserve quirks.

nodes.label: Feature toggle cleanup
nodes.summary: Feature toggles should have owners, expiry dates, and cleanup plans. Stale toggles create hidden branches, test matrix growth, configuration risk, and dead code.

nodes.label: Code review quality
nodes.summary: Code review quality depends on reviewing behavior, risk, maintainability, tests, naming, compatibility, and operational impact. Reviews should make the change better without becoming a style-only gate.

nodes.label: Architecture decision records
nodes.summary: Architecture decision records capture the context, options, decision, and consequences of important technical choices. They help future engineers understand why a design exists before changing it.

nodes.label: Estimation and risk slicing
nodes.summary: Estimation improves when work is sliced around uncertainty, dependencies, feedback, and irreversible decisions. Risk-first slices turn unknowns into evidence before committing to a large implementation path.

nodes.label: Documentation close to code
nodes.summary: Documentation close to code keeps examples, contracts, commands, and design notes near the implementation they describe. It reduces drift when docs can be reviewed and regenerated with code changes.

nodes.label: Systematic debugging
nodes.summary: Systematic debugging forms a hypothesis, chooses the smallest useful observation, compares expected and actual behavior, and updates the model. It prevents random edits from hiding the real cause.

nodes.label: Contextual logging
nodes.summary: Contextual logging records enough stable identifiers and state to reconstruct behavior without dumping sensitive data. Good logs explain what happened, where, for whom, and why the code chose that path.

nodes.label: Configuration boundaries
nodes.summary: Configuration boundaries separate code from environment-specific values while keeping validation close to startup. Strong config boundaries prevent missing, misspelled, or incompatible settings from failing deep in runtime.

nodes.label: Performance profiling before optimization
nodes.summary: Performance profiling measures where time, memory, or I/O is actually spent before changing code. Profiling protects teams from optimizing the wrong path or trading clarity for unmeasured speed.

nodes.label: Foundations and taxonomy
nodes.note: Use this group to clarify what the design system owns, how design and engineering collaborate, and how shared UI language stays coherent across products.

nodes.label: Tokens and theming
nodes.note: Use this group to connect Figma variables, semantic tokens, code outputs, themes, and migration paths without letting visual decisions drift between tools.

nodes.label: Figma and design-code handoff
nodes.note: Use this group to make design intent inspectable and traceable through variants, responsive constraints, specs, issues, and acceptance criteria.

nodes.label: Component API and implementation
nodes.note: Use this group to translate design decisions into stable component APIs, composition models, state contracts, and styling rules.

nodes.label: Documentation, testing, and release
nodes.note: Use this group to keep component behavior documented, tested, versioned, and safe for consuming teams to upgrade.

nodes.label: Adoption and operations
nodes.note: Use this group to treat the design system as a product with roadmap, coverage, governance, package distribution, and debt management.

nodes.label: Design system purpose and governance
nodes.summary: A design system is the operating layer between product design, UI engineering, and shipped interfaces. Governance defines who can change tokens, components, Figma libraries, package APIs, documentation, and release policy.

nodes.label: Component inventory and audit
nodes.summary: A component inventory identifies repeated UI patterns, implementation variants, usage frequency, accessibility risk, and ownership gaps. It turns vague design debt into a prioritized system backlog.

nodes.label: Design language taxonomy
nodes.summary: Design language taxonomy names the primitives, patterns, templates, and product-specific exceptions in a shared vocabulary. Clear taxonomy keeps Figma names, component names, token names, and documentation aligned.

nodes.label: Accessibility as a design constraint
nodes.summary: Accessibility belongs in design decisions before implementation. Color contrast, focus order, target size, motion, labels, keyboard behavior, and error messaging should be treated as design constraints, not late QA fixes.

nodes.label: Contribution model and ownership
nodes.summary: A contribution model explains how teams propose, review, build, document, and release system changes. It defines ownership across design, engineering, accessibility, product, and platform maintainers.

nodes.label: Design token architecture
nodes.summary: Design token architecture separates raw values, semantic decisions, component aliases, and platform outputs. This lets a color, spacing, typography, or motion decision move from design source to code without hardcoded drift.

nodes.label: Token naming and semantic layers
nodes.summary: Token names should encode intent rather than current visual appearance. Semantic layers such as surface, text, border, action, and feedback survive rebrands better than names like blue-500 or gray-light.

nodes.label: Figma variables to code tokens
nodes.summary: Figma variables become reliable code tokens only when naming, modes, aliases, exports, review, and versioning are explicit. The pipeline should detect missing mappings before app code consumes broken values.

nodes.label: Theme modes and brand theming
nodes.summary: Theme modes map the same semantic token names to different values for light, dark, high-contrast, brand, or tenant contexts. The component API should consume stable semantics, not mode-specific literals.

nodes.label: Token versioning and migration
nodes.summary: Token versioning protects consuming apps when a token is renamed, removed, or changes meaning. Migration notes, aliases, deprecation windows, and codemods keep design changes from becoming scattered UI regressions.

nodes.label: Figma component variants
nodes.summary: Figma variants model the supported visual states and options for a component. They should map closely to code props so designers and engineers are discussing the same combinations and constraints.

nodes.label: Auto layout and responsive constraints
nodes.summary: Auto layout and responsive constraints make design intent explicit for spacing, wrapping, alignment, truncation, and resizing. They reduce ambiguity when a Figma frame becomes real CSS layout.

nodes.label: Design spec handoff quality
nodes.summary: Design handoff quality depends on states, content rules, accessibility notes, responsive behavior, data edge cases, and interaction timing. A polished static frame is not enough to implement durable UI.

nodes.label: GitHub issues for design changes
nodes.summary: GitHub issues connect design requests to engineering review, implementation, tests, release notes, and linked Figma evidence. They make design system changes traceable instead of scattered across comments and chat.

nodes.label: Design review acceptance criteria
nodes.summary: Design review acceptance criteria define what must be true before a component change ships: visual match, accessible behavior, documented states, responsive behavior, analytics impact, and migration guidance.

nodes.label: Component prop API design
nodes.summary: Component prop APIs translate design intent into reusable engineering interfaces. Good APIs expose stable semantic choices, prevent invalid combinations, and leave room for content and accessibility requirements.

nodes.label: Slots composition and escape hatches
nodes.summary: Slots and composition let product teams place custom content inside system components without forking them. Escape hatches should be deliberate, documented, and constrained so they do not undermine consistency.

nodes.label: Controlled vs uncontrolled components
nodes.summary: Controlled components let app state own the value, while uncontrolled components keep internal state until a boundary event. Design system components should choose the model that matches validation, form, and composition needs.

nodes.label: Visual states and interaction contracts
nodes.summary: Visual states such as hover, focus, disabled, loading, selected, invalid, and pressed are interaction contracts. They should be represented in design, documentation, tests, and implementation with the same names.

nodes.label: Styling strategy for component libraries
nodes.summary: A component library styling strategy decides how tokens, CSS variables, cascade layers, class names, composition, and app overrides interact. The strategy should protect consistency while allowing product-specific layout.

nodes.label: Storybook-driven documentation
nodes.summary: Storybook-style documentation pairs component examples with props, states, accessibility notes, tokens, and usage guidance. It becomes a shared review surface for design, engineering, QA, and product teams.

nodes.label: Visual regression testing
nodes.summary: Visual regression testing compares rendered component states across changes to catch unintended appearance shifts. It is most useful when snapshots represent real supported states instead of random page screenshots.

nodes.label: Interaction and accessibility tests
nodes.summary: Interaction and accessibility tests verify keyboard flow, focus management, ARIA state, labels, disabled behavior, and event timing. They protect behavior that visual review alone cannot reliably catch.

nodes.label: Changelog and release notes for components
nodes.summary: Component changelogs explain what changed, why it changed, what apps must update, and whether visual or behavioral snapshots should be reviewed. They make design system releases consumable by product teams.

nodes.label: Deprecation and migration playbooks
nodes.summary: Deprecation playbooks give teams a path away from old tokens, props, variants, or components. Good migrations include timelines, warnings, codemods, examples, support windows, and removal criteria.

nodes.label: Adoption metrics and coverage
nodes.summary: Adoption metrics show where the design system is used, bypassed, forked, or missing. Coverage data helps prioritize components, migrations, docs, and support work based on real product impact.

nodes.label: Cross-team design system roadmap
nodes.summary: A cross-team roadmap balances product needs, accessibility fixes, token migrations, component quality, design language evolution, and platform investment. It keeps the system from becoming only a component backlog.

nodes.label: Design debt triage
nodes.summary: Design debt triage ranks inconsistent UI, missing states, token drift, inaccessible patterns, and local component forks by user impact and implementation cost. It turns inconsistency into managed product debt.

nodes.label: Governance between Figma and GitHub
nodes.summary: Figma and GitHub governance defines how design decisions become reviewed code changes, packages, docs, and releases. The goal is traceable alignment between the design source of truth and shipped UI components.

nodes.label: Package distribution and consuming apps
nodes.summary: Design system packages must work for consuming apps with clear peer dependencies, build outputs, versioning, tree shaking, CSS loading, and upgrade guidance. Distribution quality determines whether teams can adopt the system safely.

nodes.label: Transport and protocol internals
nodes.note: Use this group to reason about how bytes move over the network, what happens under packet loss, and where protocol-level latency or head-of-line blocking comes from.

nodes.label: Deployment and reliability patterns
nodes.note: Use this group to keep systems available while code, traffic, dependencies, and failure modes change.

nodes.label: Databases, storage, and transactions
nodes.note: Use this group to connect correctness guarantees to indexes, query plans, isolation, locks, replication, and storage-engine behavior.

nodes.label: Distributed systems and consistency
nodes.note: Use this group to reason about partitions, locks, consensus, conflict resolution, idempotency, and exactly-once claims.

nodes.label: Messaging, streams, and event-driven systems
nodes.note: Use this group to design event pipelines that survive retries, reordering, backpressure, projection lag, and consumer failures.

nodes.label: API design, auth, and edge controls
nodes.note: Use this group to make APIs safe, compatible, observable, throttled, cacheable, and resilient under N+1, auth, schema, or gateway pressure.

nodes.label: Observability and operations
nodes.note: Use this group to make production behavior debuggable with traces, logs, metrics, cardinality control, sampling, and chaos experiments.

nodes.label: Runtime, OS, and performance engineering
nodes.note: Use this group to reason about memory, CPU, syscalls, worker pools, event loops, atomics, lock-free algorithms, and zero-copy paths.

nodes.label: Cloud, containers, and service topology
nodes.note: Use this group to model platform primitives like service meshes, discovery, sidecars, serverless, Kubernetes disruption controls, and container hardening.

nodes.label: Caching, hashing, and approximate data structures
nodes.note: Use this group to design fast paths that remain correct enough under invalidation, shard movement, cardinality estimation, and hot-key pressure.

nodes.label: TCP congestion control algorithms
nodes.summary: TCP congestion control adjusts send rate based on acknowledgements, loss, and inferred network capacity. A clear answer mentions slow start, congestion avoidance, multiplicative decrease, RTT, packet loss, and fairness.

nodes.label: TLS 1.3 handshake internals
nodes.summary: TLS 1.3 reduces handshake round trips and encrypts more of the negotiation than TLS 1.2. Key concepts are ClientHello, key share, certificate verification, Finished messages, forward secrecy, and optional 0-RTT replay risk.

nodes.label: HTTP/2 multiplexing & HPACK
nodes.summary: HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection and compresses headers with HPACK dynamic tables. It removes HTTP/1.1 request queueing but can still suffer TCP-level head-of-line blocking.

nodes.label: HTTP/3 + QUIC packet loss recovery
nodes.summary: HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP, combining TLS 1.3, multiplexed streams, connection migration, and per-stream loss recovery. Packet loss no longer blocks unrelated streams the same way HTTP/2 over TCP can.

nodes.label: Connection pooling pitfalls
nodes.summary: Connection pools reduce setup cost but can fail through exhaustion, stale sockets, head-of-line blocking, uneven load, leaks, or pool sizes that exceed database/server limits. Correct sizing and timeout behavior matter.

nodes.label: Zero-downtime deployment strategies
nodes.summary: Zero-downtime deployment keeps traffic served while replacing code. Common techniques include readiness probes, draining, blue-green, canary, backward-compatible schemas, feature flags, and fast rollback.

nodes.label: Database transaction isolation levels (serializable vs snapshot)
nodes.summary: Isolation levels define which concurrent transaction anomalies are possible. Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a consistent view but can allow write skew; serializable aims to behave as if transactions ran one at a time.

nodes.label: B-tree vs LSM-tree index internals
nodes.summary: B-trees maintain ordered pages for efficient point and range reads, while LSM-trees buffer writes and compact sorted files later. The trade-off is read amplification versus write throughput and compaction cost.

nodes.label: Query planner & cost-based optimization
nodes.summary: A cost-based query planner estimates alternative execution plans using statistics, selectivity, join order, index availability, and I/O/CPU costs. Bad stats or parameter skew can produce poor plans.

nodes.label: Deadlock detection & prevention
nodes.summary: Deadlocks occur when transactions wait on each other in a cycle. Databases detect cycles in wait-for graphs or prevent them with lock ordering, timeouts, smaller transactions, and consistent access patterns.

nodes.label: ACID vs BASE trade-offs
nodes.summary: ACID emphasizes atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability; BASE accepts softer consistency for availability and scalability. The real decision is which invariants must be immediately correct versus eventually reconciled.

nodes.label: Two-phase commit vs Saga pattern
nodes.summary: Two-phase commit coordinates participants for atomic commit but can block and depends on a coordinator. Sagas split work into local transactions with compensating actions, trading atomicity for availability and explicit recovery.

nodes.label: Distributed locking (Redlock pitfalls)
nodes.summary: Distributed locks are hard because clocks, partitions, pauses, and delayed clients can violate mutual exclusion. Redlock-style leases need careful TTL assumptions and often require fencing tokens to protect downstream resources.

nodes.label: CAP theorem in practice
nodes.summary: CAP says that during a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability. In practice, systems make per-operation trade-offs with leader routing, quorum reads/writes, retries, and degraded modes.

nodes.label: CRDTs & conflict-free replicated data types
nodes.summary: CRDTs let replicas update independently and merge deterministically without coordination. Backend use cases include counters, sets, presence, collaborative state, and eventually consistent multi-region writes.

nodes.label: Eventual consistency anti-patterns
nodes.summary: Eventual consistency becomes an anti-pattern when product flows require immediate guarantees but the system hides lag. Examples include stale permission reads, double spends, missing read-your-writes, and silent conflict overwrites.

nodes.label: Kafka partition rebalancing & exactly-once semantics
nodes.summary: Kafka rebalancing moves partitions across consumers when group membership changes, causing pauses and offset coordination. Exactly-once semantics rely on idempotent producers, transactions, committed offsets, and careful sink behavior.

nodes.label: RabbitMQ dead-letter queues & message ordering
nodes.summary: RabbitMQ dead-letter queues capture rejected, expired, or failed messages for later handling. Ordering can be broken by retries, multiple consumers, requeueing, priorities, and dead-letter routing.

nodes.label: gRPC streaming + flow control
nodes.summary: gRPC streaming sends multiple messages over HTTP/2 streams with flow control. A good explanation covers client/server/bidirectional streams, backpressure, message framing, deadlines, cancellation, and per-stream windows.

nodes.label: GraphQL resolver batching & N+1 problem
nodes.group: API design, auth, and edge controls
nodes.summary: The GraphQL N+1 problem happens when nested resolvers issue one backend query per parent object. Batching and caching loaders group keys per tick or request to reduce queries while preserving resolver composition.

nodes.label: OAuth2 token introspection vs JWT validation
nodes.group: API design, auth, and edge controls
nodes.summary: JWT validation checks signed claims locally, while token introspection asks the authorization server whether a token is active. JWTs reduce latency but are harder to revoke instantly; introspection centralizes truth but adds network dependency.

nodes.label: Rate limiting algorithms (token bucket vs leaky bucket)
nodes.group: API design, auth, and edge controls
nodes.summary: Token bucket allows bursts up to bucket capacity while refilling over time; leaky bucket smooths output at a fixed rate. The right choice depends on burst tolerance, fairness, and user experience.

nodes.label: Circuit breaker + bulkhead patterns
nodes.summary: Circuit breakers stop calling failing dependencies temporarily; bulkheads isolate resource pools so one failing area does not exhaust the entire service. Together they prevent cascading failures.

nodes.label: Observability: OpenTelemetry tracing propagation
nodes.summary: Tracing propagation carries trace and span context across service boundaries. OpenTelemetry standardizes context extraction/injection so logs, metrics, and spans can be correlated across distributed requests.

nodes.label: Prometheus metric cardinality explosion
nodes.summary: Cardinality explosion happens when labels create too many unique time series. User IDs, raw URLs, emails, request IDs, and high-cardinality dimensions can make Prometheus expensive or unusable.

nodes.label: Log aggregation with sampling
nodes.summary: Log sampling reduces volume while preserving important signals. Good policies keep all errors/security events, sample noisy success paths, and attach trace IDs so sampled logs still join a request story.

nodes.label: Memory-mapped files vs traditional I/O
nodes.summary: Memory-mapped files map file pages into process address space, letting the OS page data in lazily. Traditional I/O copies through explicit buffers. Node does not expose mmap directly, so streams and buffers are the usual tools.

nodes.label: Garbage collection tuning (G1 vs ZGC)
nodes.summary: G1 and ZGC are JVM collectors with different pause/throughput trade-offs; in Node the analogous topic is V8 heap sizing and GC behavior. Strong explanations separate allocation rate, live set, pause time, and throughput.

nodes.label: Thread pools vs virtual threads (Project Loom)
nodes.summary: Thread pools bound scarce OS threads; virtual threads multiplex many blocking-style tasks onto fewer carrier threads in the JVM. In Node, the closest contrast is async I/O plus worker threads for CPU-bound work.

nodes.label: Actor model vs shared-memory concurrency
nodes.summary: The actor model isolates state behind message queues, while shared-memory concurrency shares mutable state with locks or atomics. Actors simplify reasoning but require backpressure and message ordering design.

nodes.label: Message-driven architecture (Akka / Orleans)
nodes.summary: Message-driven architecture structures systems around asynchronous messages and handlers. It improves decoupling and resilience but introduces delivery guarantees, ordering, retries, idempotency, and observability requirements.

nodes.label: CQRS + Event Sourcing projections
nodes.summary: CQRS separates command writes from query reads, and event sourcing records state changes as events. Projections build read models from those events and must handle replay, lag, schema changes, and idempotency.

nodes.label: Outbox pattern for reliable events
nodes.summary: The outbox pattern writes domain data and an event record in the same database transaction, then a relay publishes the event. It avoids losing events between DB commit and broker publish.

nodes.label: Sharding strategies & hot partition avoidance
nodes.summary: Sharding splits data across partitions by key, range, hash, tenant, or geography. Hot partitions happen when too much traffic targets one shard and are mitigated with better keys, salting, splitting, and load-aware routing.

nodes.label: Read replicas lag monitoring
nodes.summary: Read replica lag is the delay between primary writes and replica visibility. Monitoring should track replication position/time lag and route read-your-writes or critical reads to fresh sources when needed.

nodes.label: Database connection pool exhaustion
nodes.summary: Pool exhaustion occurs when all DB connections are busy or leaked. Symptoms include request pileups, timeouts, and cascading latency; fixes include smaller transactions, timeouts, queue limits, and right-sized pools.

nodes.label: Prepared statement caching
nodes.summary: Prepared statement caching reuses parsed/planned SQL statements to reduce overhead and improve safety. Pitfalls include unbounded caches, schema changes, connection-specific state, and bad generic plans.

nodes.label: Index bloat & vacuum strategies
nodes.summary: Index bloat is wasted index space from dead or outdated entries, common in MVCC systems. Vacuuming, autovacuum tuning, fillfactor choices, and periodic reindexing control space and planner quality.

nodes.label: Kubernetes pod disruption budgets
nodes.summary: Pod disruption budgets limit voluntary disruptions so enough replicas remain available during drains, upgrades, or maintenance. They are useful only when paired with enough replicas, readiness probes, and capacity.

nodes.label: Service mesh traffic shifting
nodes.summary: Service mesh traffic shifting routes percentages of traffic between versions or services using proxy control planes. It supports canary, blue-green, retries, and mTLS, but adds latency, complexity, and debugging surface.

nodes.label: Serverless cold-start mitigation
nodes.summary: Cold starts happen when a serverless runtime initializes before handling a request. Mitigation includes smaller bundles, hoisted clients, lazy initialization, provisioned concurrency, and avoiding heavy startup work.

nodes.label: API gateway throttling & caching layers
nodes.group: API design, auth, and edge controls
nodes.summary: API gateways enforce cross-cutting policies such as auth, rate limits, request validation, caching, and routing. Caching must vary on identity, authorization, headers, and query shape to avoid data leaks.

nodes.label: Background job queues (Celery / BullMQ) retry semantics
nodes.summary: Job queues need explicit retry, backoff, dead-letter, timeout, and idempotency semantics. Without them, jobs can duplicate side effects, poison queues, or hide permanent failures behind endless retries.

nodes.label: Distributed cache invalidation (cache-aside vs write-through)
nodes.group: Caching, hashing, and approximate data structures
nodes.summary: Cache-aside loads on miss and invalidates after writes; write-through writes cache and database together. Distributed invalidation must handle races, partial failures, versioning, and cross-node propagation delay.

nodes.label: Eventual consistency in cache
nodes.group: Caching, hashing, and approximate data structures
nodes.summary: Eventually consistent caches can serve stale data after writes, invalidations, or replication delays. Safe design scopes staleness, uses versions, routes critical reads to truth, and avoids caching irreversible authorization decisions incorrectly.

nodes.label: Idempotency keys in API design
nodes.summary: Idempotency keys let clients safely retry state-changing requests without creating duplicate side effects. The server stores the key, request fingerprint, status, and response for a defined retention window.

nodes.label: Optimistic locking with version vectors
nodes.summary: Optimistic locking detects conflicts by comparing a version or vector before write commit. Version vectors track causal progress across replicas and can distinguish stale writes from concurrent writes.

nodes.label: Paxos / Raft consensus internals
nodes.summary: Consensus protocols let distributed nodes agree on ordered state despite failures. Raft explains this through leader election, terms, logs, majorities, commit indexes, and safety rules.

nodes.label: Byzantine fault tolerance basics
nodes.summary: Byzantine fault tolerance handles nodes that can lie, collude, or behave arbitrarily. Classic BFT requires more replicas than crash fault tolerance, commonly 3f+1 replicas to tolerate f Byzantine faults.

nodes.label: Chaos engineering principles
nodes.summary: Chaos engineering tests resilience by injecting controlled failures into production-like systems. It should start with hypotheses, blast-radius limits, rollback, observability, and learning from the result.

nodes.label: Database failover & split-brain prevention
nodes.summary: Failover promotes a standby when primary fails; split-brain occurs when multiple primaries accept writes. Prevention uses quorum, fencing tokens, leases, STONITH-style isolation, and conservative promotion rules.

nodes.label: Microservices observability (distributed tracing)
nodes.summary: Distributed tracing follows one request across services, queues, and databases. It requires context propagation, span naming discipline, sampling, baggage caution, and correlation with logs and metrics.

nodes.label: API contract testing (Pact / Spring Cloud Contract)
nodes.group: API design, auth, and edge controls
nodes.summary: Contract testing verifies that providers and consumers agree on request/response behavior. It catches breaking changes earlier than full integration tests and supports independent service deployment.

nodes.label: Backward-compatible schema evolution
nodes.group: API design, auth, and edge controls
nodes.summary: Backward-compatible schema evolution changes APIs or events without breaking old consumers. Common moves are additive fields, default values, tolerant readers, deprecation windows, and dual-read/write migrations.

nodes.label: Protobuf vs JSON performance trade-offs
nodes.group: API design, auth, and edge controls
nodes.summary: Protobuf is compact, typed, and schema-driven; JSON is human-readable and ubiquitous. Trade-offs include payload size, CPU parse cost, compatibility rules, introspection, tooling, and browser/debug ergonomics.

nodes.label: Binary protocol parsing
nodes.summary: Binary protocol parsing reads structured fields from byte buffers using offsets, endianness, lengths, and framing rules. Correct parsers defend against partial frames, oversized lengths, and malicious input.

nodes.label: Zero-copy networking (sendfile)
nodes.summary: Zero-copy networking avoids copying file data through user-space buffers, often with sendfile-like kernel paths. Node typically approximates this with efficient streams, though true sendfile exposure depends on runtime/platform.

nodes.label: epoll / kqueue internals
nodes.summary: epoll and kqueue are OS event notification mechanisms for scalable nonblocking I/O. Node relies on libuv abstractions over these primitives to drive sockets, timers, and file events.

nodes.label: Syscall overhead & context switching
nodes.summary: System calls and context switches cross boundaries between user space, kernel space, and runnable tasks. Batching, buffering, async I/O, and fewer tiny writes reduce overhead.

nodes.label: Memory barriers & CPU cache coherence
nodes.summary: Memory barriers constrain how CPU cores reorder reads/writes so shared-memory programs observe safe ordering. In JavaScript, Atomics operations on SharedArrayBuffer provide the relevant synchronization primitives.

nodes.label: Lock-free data structures
nodes.summary: Lock-free data structures use atomic operations instead of mutexes so system-wide progress continues even if one thread stalls. They are hard to design because of ABA, memory ordering, and contention.

nodes.label: Bloom filters & HyperLogLog in practice
nodes.group: Caching, hashing, and approximate data structures
nodes.summary: Bloom filters answer maybe-present/definitely-not-present with false positives; HyperLogLog estimates cardinality with small memory. Both trade exactness for speed and memory efficiency.

nodes.label: Consistent hashing for load balancing
nodes.group: Caching, hashing, and approximate data structures
nodes.summary: Consistent hashing maps keys to nodes so adding or removing nodes moves only a fraction of keys. It is useful for caches, shards, and load balancing with reduced remapping churn.

nodes.label: Virtual memory & page faults impact
nodes.summary: Virtual memory lets processes use address spaces backed by physical memory and disk. Page faults occur when needed pages are not resident, causing latency from allocation, disk, or OS bookkeeping.

nodes.label: Container runtime security (seccomp, AppArmor)
nodes.summary: Container runtime security restricts what a process can do despite sharing the host kernel. seccomp filters syscalls, AppArmor/SELinux constrain access, and least-privilege settings reduce blast radius.

nodes.label: Sidecar pattern limitations
nodes.summary: Sidecars add colocated helper processes for proxying, logging, security, or config. Limitations include extra hops, resource overhead, lifecycle coupling, harder debugging, and duplicated functionality per pod.

nodes.label: Service discovery (Consul vs DNS)
nodes.summary: Service discovery maps logical service names to healthy instances. DNS is simple and ubiquitous; Consul-style systems can add health checks, metadata, watches, and stronger service catalog semantics.

nodes.label: Blue-green vs canary deployments
nodes.summary: Blue-green switches traffic between two full environments; canary gradually shifts a small percentage to a new version. Blue-green is simpler rollback, while canary gives safer progressive exposure.

nodes.label: Feature flags with rollout strategies
nodes.summary: Feature flags decouple deploy from release and allow targeting, gradual rollout, kill switches, and experiments. Good systems need stable bucketing, auditability, cleanup, and dependency management.

nodes.label: Data pipeline backpressure handling
nodes.summary: Pipeline backpressure prevents upstream producers from overwhelming downstream consumers. It is implemented with bounded queues, credits, pull-based reads, pause/resume, rate limits, and load shedding.

nodes.label: Exactly-once processing guarantees
nodes.summary: Exactly-once usually means effects are applied once through idempotency and transactions, not that messages are delivered once. Strong answers distinguish delivery, processing, side effects, offsets, and sink commits.

nodes.label: Idempotent consumers in event streams
nodes.summary: Idempotent consumers handle duplicate events safely by recording processed IDs, using natural keys, checking versions, or making writes commutative. This is required because retries and rebalances can redeliver messages.

nodes.label: Design process and trade-offs
nodes.note: Use this group to turn product goals into explicit requirements, constraints, trade-offs, and decisions that can be revisited later.

nodes.label: Scale, capacity, and latency
nodes.note: Use this group to size traffic, storage, throughput, latency budgets, queues, caches, and concurrency before selecting technology.

nodes.label: Boundaries and topology
nodes.note: Use this group to place client, edge, API, service, data, control-plane, and data-plane responsibilities deliberately.

nodes.label: Data, consistency, and workflows
nodes.note: Use this group to connect access patterns, consistency needs, partitions, freshness, events, and workflow recovery into one design.

nodes.label: Reliability and operations
nodes.note: Use this group to reason about failure modes, overload behavior, fallback, disaster recovery, observability, alerts, and releases.

nodes.label: Security, abuse, and governance
nodes.note: Use this group to protect system boundaries, secrets, tenants, quotas, abuse paths, and operational policy surfaces.

nodes.label: Cost, evolution, and decision records
nodes.note: Use this group to keep architecture economically grounded and evolvable through buy/build calls, migrations, and recorded decisions.

nodes.label: Functional vs non-functional requirements
nodes.summary: Functional requirements describe what the system must do, while non-functional requirements describe qualities such as latency, availability, privacy, durability, scale, and cost. Senior design work makes both explicit before choosing components.

nodes.label: SLOs and error budgets
nodes.summary: SLOs define target reliability for user-visible behavior, while error budgets quantify how much unreliability the system can spend. They turn vague reliability goals into decisions about release pace, alerting, redundancy, and degradation.

nodes.label: Capacity estimation
nodes.summary: Capacity estimation turns traffic, payload size, storage retention, fanout, and peak multipliers into concrete throughput and storage numbers. The goal is not perfect prediction; it is making bottlenecks and scaling assumptions visible.

nodes.label: Latency budget decomposition
nodes.summary: A latency budget splits an end-to-end target across client work, network hops, edge logic, services, databases, queues, and third-party calls. It helps identify where parallelism, caching, streaming, or simplification is required.

nodes.label: Client-edge-service boundaries
nodes.summary: Client, edge, and service boundaries decide where validation, personalization, caching, rendering, authorization, and aggregation live. Good boundaries reduce latency and coupling without leaking trusted responsibilities to untrusted environments.

nodes.label: API gateway and BFF boundaries
nodes.summary: An API gateway applies cross-cutting concerns such as auth, rate limits, caching, and routing, while a backend-for-frontend shapes APIs around a specific client experience. Mixing them carelessly can create a slow, overloaded coordination layer.

nodes.label: Read path vs write path design
nodes.summary: Read paths and write paths often need different guarantees, storage models, caches, and scaling strategies. Separating them clarifies which flows require immediate correctness and which can tolerate projection lag or denormalized views.

nodes.label: Control plane vs data plane
nodes.summary: The control plane configures policy and desired state, while the data plane handles the high-volume request or data path. Separating them keeps runtime traffic fast and resilient even when management workflows are slower or partially unavailable.

nodes.label: Data modeling from access patterns
nodes.summary: Access-pattern-first data modeling starts with queries, writes, cardinality, ordering, and consistency needs before choosing tables, documents, indexes, or streams. It prevents elegant schemas that cannot serve real traffic.

nodes.label: Cache placement and invalidation
nodes.summary: Cache placement decides whether data is cached in the browser, edge, gateway, service, database layer, or client state. Invalidation must match freshness requirements, user specificity, mutation flow, and failure behavior.

nodes.label: Partitioning and tenant isolation
nodes.summary: Partitioning splits data and traffic across shards, tenants, regions, or cells. Tenant isolation adds blast-radius control so one large or unhealthy tenant does not degrade unrelated customers.

nodes.label: Read freshness routing
nodes.summary: Read freshness routing chooses between replicas, caches, primaries, or quorum reads based on how fresh a response must be. It is the system-level version of making read-your-writes and stale-data rules explicit.

nodes.label: Async workflow design
nodes.summary: Async workflow design coordinates durable state changes across queues, jobs, events, retries, and compensations. The design must define ownership, idempotency, retry semantics, visibility, and recovery after partial progress.

nodes.label: Failure mode analysis
nodes.summary: Failure mode analysis lists what can break, how the system detects it, what user impact it creates, and which mitigation applies. It converts architecture diagrams from happy-path pictures into operable designs.

nodes.label: Backpressure and load shedding
nodes.summary: Backpressure slows producers when downstream systems are saturated, while load shedding rejects or drops work deliberately to preserve critical paths. A design should define queue limits, priorities, retry rules, and user-visible errors.

nodes.label: Degradation and fallback design
nodes.summary: Degradation and fallback design decides which features can be disabled, simplified, cached, or delayed when dependencies fail. Good fallbacks are intentional product states, not accidental error handling.

nodes.label: Disaster recovery objectives (RTO/RPO)
nodes.summary: RTO is how long recovery may take, and RPO is how much data loss is acceptable. These objectives drive backup frequency, replication, failover automation, drills, and whether the design needs active-active or active-passive recovery.

nodes.label: Operational readiness review
nodes.summary: Operational readiness checks whether a system can be deployed, observed, rolled back, debugged, scaled, secured, and supported before it handles real traffic. It is the practical bridge between design and production ownership.

nodes.label: Tracing across async workflows
nodes.summary: Tracing across async workflows carries correlation through requests, events, jobs, retries, and projections. Without it, the system can appear healthy while individual user workflows disappear between components.

nodes.label: Runbook and alert design
nodes.summary: Runbook and alert design connects symptoms to ownership, impact, first checks, mitigation, and escalation. Alerts should be tied to user impact or fast-burn risk, not every noisy internal metric.

nodes.label: Release strategy selection
nodes.summary: Release strategy selection chooses between rolling, blue-green, canary, feature flags, shadow traffic, and migrations based on blast radius, reversibility, data compatibility, and confidence signals.

nodes.label: Threat modeling at system boundaries
nodes.summary: Threat modeling at system boundaries identifies trust zones, entry points, assets, attackers, and mitigations. It keeps security connected to architecture instead of treating it as a checklist after implementation.

nodes.label: Abuse and quota controls
nodes.summary: Abuse and quota controls protect systems from spam, scraping, brute force, runaway automation, and unfair resource use. Effective designs combine identity, rate limits, quotas, anomaly detection, and appeal paths.

nodes.label: Secret and configuration boundaries
nodes.summary: Secret and configuration boundaries define where credentials, feature flags, tenant settings, and runtime policy may live. A safe design prevents secrets from leaking to clients, logs, traces, build artifacts, or untrusted plugins.

nodes.label: Cost-aware architecture
nodes.summary: Cost-aware architecture models the cost drivers of traffic, storage, compute, egress, third-party APIs, observability, and operational effort. It does not mean choosing the cheapest path; it means making cost part of the design trade-off.

nodes.label: Build vs buy evaluation
nodes.summary: Build vs buy evaluation compares capability fit, integration risk, lock-in, security, operations, support, cost curves, and strategic differentiation. The useful answer is often a staged decision, not a permanent ideology.

nodes.label: Migration and strangler patterns
nodes.summary: Migration and strangler patterns replace systems incrementally by routing slices of traffic or capability to the new path while the old path keeps running. The design must include parity checks, rollback, data sync, and ownership boundaries.

nodes.label: Architecture decision records
nodes.summary: Architecture decision records capture context, decision, alternatives, consequences, and revisit triggers. They preserve the reasoning behind trade-offs so future engineers can change direction without rediscovering old constraints.

nodes.label: LLM fundamentals and model behavior
nodes.note: Use this group to understand how model limits, sampling, latency, throughput, and capability fit affect production AI features.

nodes.label: Prompting and context engineering
nodes.note: Use this group to assemble instructions, variables, examples, source context, and conversation state without losing control of the task.

nodes.label: Structured outputs and tool use
nodes.note: Use this group to make model interactions machine-checkable with schemas, tool contracts, validation, dispatch, and permission boundaries.

nodes.label: Retrieval and knowledge grounding
nodes.note: Use this group to connect embeddings, chunking, metadata, retrieval, reranking, and source-of-truth rules into grounded answers.

nodes.label: Evaluation and observability
nodes.note: Use this group to measure AI behavior with datasets, traces, prompt regression tests, judge calibration, and production quality signals.

nodes.label: Safety, security, and data handling
nodes.note: Use this group to reduce prompt injection, unsafe output, privacy leakage, and unclear escalation behavior in AI-backed systems.

nodes.label: Agentic workflows
nodes.note: Use this group to design loops that plan, act, observe, persist state, ask for human review, and recover from partial progress.

nodes.label: Model operations, cost, and rollout
nodes.note: Use this group to route models, control cost, cache safely, stream responses, and roll out AI features with measurable risk.

nodes.label: Tokens and context windows
nodes.summary: Tokens are the model's input and output units, and the context window is the bounded working set the model can attend to. Practical AI engineering treats context as a scarce budget shared by instructions, user input, retrieved sources, tools, and output.

nodes.label: Sampling, temperature, and top-p
nodes.summary: Sampling settings change how the model chooses among likely next tokens. Temperature affects sharpness, top-p limits the candidate probability mass, and both must be tuned around task type, determinism needs, and evaluation signals.

nodes.label: Model capability fit
nodes.summary: Model capability fit matches a task to a model based on reasoning depth, tool use, latency, context length, language coverage, multimodal needs, cost, and safety behavior. The best model is the one that meets the product constraint, not always the largest model.

nodes.label: Latency, throughput, and batching
nodes.summary: AI latency includes queueing, prompt assembly, model time, streaming cadence, tool calls, and post-processing. Throughput work often introduces batching or caching, which must be balanced against tail latency and personalization.

nodes.label: Instruction hierarchy
nodes.summary: Instruction hierarchy defines which instructions outrank others, such as system policy, developer intent, tool constraints, retrieved content, and user requests. It is the foundation for keeping model behavior stable when context contains conflicting text.

nodes.label: Prompt templates and variables
nodes.summary: Prompt templates separate fixed instructions from dynamic variables, making prompts easier to test, version, localize, and audit. Safe templates escape or delimit untrusted inputs so data is not confused with instructions.

nodes.label: Context pruning and summarization
nodes.summary: Context pruning chooses what to keep, compress, or drop as a conversation or task grows. Good pruning preserves goals, constraints, current state, source citations, and unresolved decisions instead of blindly keeping recent messages.

nodes.label: Few-shot examples
nodes.summary: Few-shot examples demonstrate the target input-output pattern inside the prompt. They are most useful when they cover edge cases, failure modes, tone, structure, or domain-specific transformations that plain instructions underspecify.

nodes.label: JSON schema constrained output
nodes.summary: Schema-constrained output makes model responses machine-checkable by defining required fields, types, enums, arrays, and nesting. It reduces parser fragility, but downstream code must still validate and handle refusals or partial failures.

nodes.label: Tool calling contracts
nodes.summary: Tool calling contracts define the names, arguments, permissions, side effects, return values, and error semantics of tools the model may request. Strong contracts keep the model as a planner while application code remains the executor.

nodes.label: Tool dispatch and validation
nodes.summary: Tool dispatch maps model-requested tool calls to allowed application functions after validating tool name, arguments, permissions, and expected side effects. Dispatch code is a security boundary, not just plumbing.

nodes.label: Tool permission boundaries
nodes.summary: Tool permission boundaries restrict what the model can cause the system to read, write, spend, send, delete, or expose. Permission should be based on user authorization, task context, tool risk, and confirmation requirements.

nodes.label: Embeddings and cosine similarity
nodes.summary: Embeddings map text or other content into vectors so semantic similarity can be searched. Cosine similarity is a common scoring method, but retrieval quality also depends on chunking, metadata, filters, freshness, and reranking.

nodes.label: Chunking and metadata strategy
nodes.summary: Chunking splits source material into retrieval units, while metadata carries source, ownership, freshness, access control, hierarchy, and document structure. Bad chunking can make good embeddings look weak.

nodes.label: RAG retrieval pipeline
nodes.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation pulls relevant source material into model context before generation. A production RAG pipeline includes indexing, filtering, retrieval, reranking, source packing, answer generation, and citation or grounding checks.

nodes.label: Reranking and hybrid search
nodes.summary: Reranking reorders retrieved candidates using a stronger relevance signal, while hybrid search combines lexical and vector retrieval. These techniques improve grounding when semantic search alone misses exact terms, IDs, or rare phrases.

nodes.label: Conversation memory vs source of truth
nodes.summary: Conversation memory is the model-facing summary of interaction state, while the source of truth is the durable system record. Designs should avoid letting generated summaries silently overwrite authoritative data.

nodes.label: Golden set evals
nodes.summary: Golden set evals use curated examples with expected behavior to measure prompt, model, retrieval, and tool changes. Good sets include common cases, edge cases, regressions, and unacceptable outputs.

nodes.label: LLM-as-judge pitfalls
nodes.summary: LLM-as-judge evals can scale qualitative review, but judges have bias, drift, prompt sensitivity, and blind spots. They need calibration against human labels, clear rubrics, disagreement tracking, and spot checks.

nodes.label: Trace logging for AI features
nodes.summary: AI traces record prompts, model choices, tool calls, retrieval inputs, outputs, latency, cost, and policy decisions with sensitive data controls. They are required to debug quality regressions and production incidents.

nodes.label: Prompt regression testing
nodes.summary: Prompt regression testing checks that prompt, model, tool, or retrieval changes do not break known behavior. The useful unit is the whole AI interaction contract, not just prompt text.

nodes.label: Prompt injection defense
nodes.summary: Prompt injection defense treats retrieved content, web pages, documents, and user text as untrusted data that may contain instructions. Defenses include instruction hierarchy, source isolation, tool permission checks, allowlists, and confirmation gates.

nodes.label: Output guardrails
nodes.summary: Output guardrails validate model responses before display, execution, storage, or sending. They can enforce schema, policy, unsafe-content checks, citation requirements, numeric bounds, or human review.

nodes.label: PII redaction and data minimization
nodes.summary: PII redaction and data minimization reduce sensitive data exposure in prompts, logs, traces, evals, and vendor calls. The safest token is the one never sent, logged, or retained unnecessarily.

nodes.label: Refusal and escalation paths
nodes.summary: Refusal and escalation paths define what the product does when the model cannot safely or confidently complete a request. Good designs preserve user trust with clear alternatives, support handoff, or constrained partial help.

nodes.label: Agent loop design
nodes.summary: An agent loop repeatedly observes state, decides next action, calls tools, records results, and stops when the goal is complete or blocked. The hard parts are stopping criteria, state, permissions, retries, and recovery.

nodes.label: Plan-execute-observe cycles
nodes.summary: Plan-execute-observe cycles split agent work into an explicit plan, bounded actions, and evidence-based updates. They help keep long tasks auditable and prevent the agent from drifting away from the objective.

nodes.label: Human-in-the-loop checkpoints
nodes.summary: Human-in-the-loop checkpoints pause an AI workflow before high-risk actions, ambiguous decisions, expensive operations, or irreversible side effects. They should be placed by risk, not sprinkled everywhere.

nodes.label: Long-running task state
nodes.summary: Long-running task state stores objective, plan, decisions, tool results, unresolved blockers, budgets, and verification evidence. Without durable state, agent workflows become hard to resume, audit, or debug.

nodes.label: Model routing and fallback
nodes.summary: Model routing sends requests to different models based on task complexity, latency target, cost budget, context size, availability, safety policy, or tenant tier. Fallback should preserve correctness boundaries, not just retry anywhere.

nodes.label: Cost controls and response caching
nodes.summary: Cost controls for AI systems include token budgets, model routing, prompt trimming, batch processing, response caching, tenant quotas, and observability. Caching is safest for deterministic, non-user-specific, policy-stable outputs.

nodes.label: Streaming AI UX
nodes.summary: Streaming AI UX delivers partial output as it is generated, improving perceived latency and enabling cancellation. It must handle partial sentences, tool-call pauses, errors, moderation, and final-state reconciliation.

nodes.label: AI feature rollout
nodes.summary: AI feature rollout introduces model-backed behavior gradually with flags, eval gates, tracing, human review, fallback, and cost monitoring. Rollout plans should account for quality drift as well as uptime.

nodes.label: Relational modeling and SQL
nodes.note: Use this group to design schemas, constraints, query shapes, and relational access patterns that stay understandable as data grows.

nodes.label: Indexing and query performance
nodes.note: Use this group to connect query plans, index design, statistics, memory, and workload shape to practical performance outcomes.

nodes.label: Transactions, migrations, and integrity
nodes.note: Use this group to protect correctness while schema, code, data volume, and concurrent writes change.

nodes.label: Storage topology and replication
nodes.note: Use this group to reason about partitioning, replicas, backups, search indexes, time-series storage, and tenant boundaries.

nodes.label: Analytics, pipelines, and governance
nodes.note: Use this group to move data into analytical systems with clear semantics, quality checks, lineage, and retention rules.

nodes.label: Relational schema design
nodes.summary: Relational schema design maps domain entities, relationships, constraints, and access patterns into tables that can preserve integrity over time. Good design uses keys, constraints, naming, cardinality, and ownership boundaries deliberately.

nodes.label: SQL joins and query shape
nodes.summary: SQL joins combine rows across tables, but query shape determines cardinality, duplicate rows, filter placement, and whether the database can use indexes. Engineers should explain inner, outer, semi, and anti joins from result semantics first.

nodes.label: Normalization vs denormalization
nodes.summary: Normalization reduces duplication and update anomalies, while denormalization duplicates data to speed reads or simplify access. The trade-off is correctness and write complexity versus query performance and product latency.

nodes.label: Data integrity constraints
nodes.summary: Data integrity constraints make correctness durable inside the database through primary keys, foreign keys, unique constraints, checks, not-null rules, and exclusion constraints. They protect invariants even when application code has bugs.

nodes.label: Temporal data modeling
nodes.summary: Temporal modeling captures when facts are valid, when the system learned them, and how history changes. It matters for auditability, pricing, entitlement windows, late-arriving updates, and reproducible analytics.

nodes.label: Index selection and covering indexes
nodes.summary: Index selection matches workload filters, joins, ordering, uniqueness, and projection columns. Covering indexes can serve a query without visiting base rows, but they increase write cost and storage.

nodes.label: Query execution plan reading
nodes.summary: Query plans show how the database intends to scan, join, sort, aggregate, and estimate row counts. Reading plans helps diagnose missing indexes, stale statistics, bad join order, and memory-heavy operations.

nodes.label: Statistics and cardinality estimation
nodes.summary: Statistics and cardinality estimates let a planner compare possible execution paths. Bad estimates from skew, correlation, stale stats, or parameter sensitivity can make reasonable SQL run poorly.

nodes.label: Connection pool sizing
nodes.summary: Connection pool sizing balances application concurrency against database capacity. Too few connections bottleneck callers; too many cause queueing, memory pressure, lock contention, and database overload.

nodes.label: Hot query and slow query triage
nodes.summary: Hot query triage identifies the queries that dominate database load by frequency, latency, rows scanned, lock wait, and memory use. Fixes can include index changes, query rewrites, caching, pagination, or product flow changes.

nodes.label: Transaction boundary design
nodes.summary: Transaction boundary design decides which reads and writes must commit atomically, how long locks are held, and what invariants need isolation. Boundaries that are too wide hurt concurrency; too narrow leak partial state.

nodes.label: Schema migration expand-contract
nodes.summary: Expand-contract migrations introduce schema changes in backward-compatible phases: expand, dual-read/write or backfill, cut over, then contract. This keeps old and new code safe during rolling deploys.

nodes.label: Online backfills
nodes.summary: Online backfills update existing data while production traffic continues. Safe backfills use batches, checkpoints, idempotency, throttling, observability, and rollback or pause behavior.

nodes.label: Optimistic concurrency control
nodes.summary: Optimistic concurrency control detects conflicting writes with versions, timestamps, compare-and-swap, or conditional updates. It works well when conflicts are rare and retry behavior is explicit.

nodes.label: Idempotent data writes
nodes.summary: Idempotent writes make retries safe by using stable operation IDs, uniqueness constraints, upserts, or processed-event tables. They are essential when clients, workers, or queues can repeat work.
