nodes.label: Partitioning and sharding strategy
nodes.summary: Partitioning and sharding split data by tenant, key, hash, range, geography, or workload. A good strategy minimizes hot partitions, cross-shard joins, rebalancing pain, and tenant blast radius.

nodes.label: Replication lag and read scaling
nodes.summary: Read replicas increase read capacity but introduce freshness lag and failover complexity. Designs must define which reads can be stale, how lag is measured, and when to route to the primary.

nodes.label: Backup, restore, and point-in-time recovery
nodes.summary: Backups only matter if restores are tested. Point-in-time recovery combines base backups and logs to restore to a chosen moment, bounded by RPO, RTO, retention, and access controls.

nodes.label: Search indexing and relevance
nodes.summary: Search indexing transforms source records into searchable documents with tokenization, ranking signals, filters, facets, and freshness rules. Search is a derived data system that needs sync and repair paths.

nodes.label: Time-series data modeling
nodes.summary: Time-series modeling optimizes append-heavy measurements with timestamps, tags, retention, rollups, downsampling, and query windows. It is common in observability, IoT, billing, and analytics.

nodes.label: OLTP vs OLAP system choice
nodes.summary: OLTP systems optimize transactional correctness and low-latency writes, while OLAP systems optimize analytical scans and aggregations. Mixing them without boundaries can hurt both product behavior and reporting.

nodes.label: CDC and event streams
nodes.summary: Change data capture turns database changes into ordered event streams for replication, search indexing, analytics, or integration. It must handle ordering, deletes, schema evolution, backfills, and replay.

nodes.label: ETL vs ELT pipelines
nodes.summary: ETL transforms before loading into the target system, while ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the analytical store. The decision changes cost, lineage, debugging, privacy, and ownership.

nodes.label: Warehouse modeling and fact tables
nodes.summary: Warehouse modeling organizes analytical data around facts, dimensions, grain, slowly changing dimensions, and business definitions. It keeps reporting consistent across teams and tools.

nodes.label: Semantic metrics layer
nodes.summary: A semantic metrics layer defines measures, dimensions, filters, windows, and ownership once so dashboards and product analysis agree. It prevents each report from inventing a different version of revenue or active users.

nodes.label: Data quality checks
nodes.summary: Data quality checks assert freshness, completeness, uniqueness, value ranges, referential integrity, and volume expectations. They catch broken ingestion or product instrumentation before decisions depend on bad data.

nodes.label: Deduplication and late-arriving data
nodes.summary: Deduplication and late-arriving data handling keep analytical results correct when events are retried, delayed, reordered, or replayed. Designs need stable IDs, watermarks, correction windows, and recomputation paths.

nodes.label: Data retention and archival policy
nodes.summary: Retention and archival policy define how long data stays hot, warm, cold, anonymized, or deleted. It balances product needs, cost, legal obligations, privacy, and restore expectations.

nodes.label: Data lineage and observability
nodes.summary: Data lineage and observability show where data came from, how it changed, when it refreshed, and what downstream assets depend on it. They are the operational controls for trusted analytical systems.

nodes.label: Vector storage and retrieval
nodes.summary: Vector storage supports similarity search over embeddings with indexes, metadata filters, refresh policies, and recall-latency trade-offs. It is useful for AI retrieval, recommendations, duplicate detection, and semantic search.

nodes.label: Source control, CI, and release automation
nodes.note: Use this group to turn changes into repeatable, reviewable, reversible delivery paths.

nodes.label: Infrastructure, environments, and cloud networking
nodes.note: Use this group to model infrastructure state, environment promotion, DNS, certificates, load balancing, and network reachability.

nodes.label: Containers, orchestration, and runtime platforms
nodes.note: Use this group to operate workloads with container hygiene, scheduling, autoscaling, service topology, and runtime constraints.

nodes.label: Security, identity, and supply chain
nodes.note: Use this group to control secrets, permissions, artifact trust, policy, and blast radius across the platform.

nodes.label: Observability, incidents, and operations
nodes.note: Use this group to make production ownership measurable, alertable, recoverable, and improvable after incidents.

nodes.label: Developer experience and platform product
nodes.note: Use this group to build internal platforms, templates, local environments, and APIs that make good engineering paths easy to follow.

nodes.label: Git workflow and branch protection
nodes.group: Source control, CI, and release automation
nodes.summary: Git workflow and branch protection define how changes move from local work to reviewed, tested, mergeable history. Useful controls include required checks, protected branches, signed commits or tags, and review ownership.

nodes.label: CI pipeline design
nodes.group: Source control, CI, and release automation
nodes.summary: CI pipeline design orders checks so fast deterministic failures happen early and expensive integration work runs only when needed. Good pipelines separate install, lint, test, build, package, and artifact verification.

nodes.label: Generated artifact drift checks
nodes.group: Source control, CI, and release automation
nodes.summary: Generated artifact drift checks run the generator in CI and fail when committed generated output is stale. This protects source-of-truth workflows without letting CI silently rewrite reviewed code.

nodes.label: Deployment strategy selection
nodes.group: Source control, CI, and release automation
nodes.summary: Deployment strategy selection chooses rolling, blue-green, canary, shadow, or feature-flagged rollout based on reversibility, data compatibility, blast radius, and signal quality.

nodes.label: Rollback and roll-forward planning
nodes.group: Source control, CI, and release automation
nodes.summary: Rollback and roll-forward planning defines what happens when a release fails. The plan must account for code, config, data migrations, caches, messages, and external side effects.

nodes.label: Infrastructure as Code state
nodes.summary: Infrastructure as Code state records the known deployed resources and their desired configuration. State must be locked, backed up, reviewed, and protected because it is a control surface for production.

nodes.label: Environment promotion
nodes.summary: Environment promotion moves the same build artifact through development, staging, and production with environment-specific config. It prevents rebuilding different binaries for each environment.

nodes.label: Cloud networking basics
nodes.summary: Cloud networking basics include VPCs, subnets, routing tables, NAT, firewalls, private endpoints, and service reachability. Platform engineers must reason about packets, identity, and policy together.

nodes.label: DNS and certificate operations
nodes.summary: DNS and certificate operations keep names resolvable and encrypted endpoints trusted. Practical knowledge includes TTLs, CNAMEs, apex records, ACME renewals, SANs, wildcard certs, and rollout timing.

nodes.label: Load balancing and health checks
nodes.summary: Load balancing distributes traffic across healthy targets, while health checks decide whether a target should receive traffic. Bad checks can amplify incidents by sending traffic to broken or warming instances.

nodes.label: Container image build hygiene
nodes.summary: Container image hygiene reduces build drift, size, vulnerabilities, and runtime privilege. Good images pin bases, avoid secrets, run as non-root, minimize layers, and separate build tools from runtime.

nodes.label: Kubernetes workload primitives
nodes.summary: Kubernetes workload primitives such as Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and Ingresses describe desired runtime state. Engineers should know what each primitive owns and does not own.

nodes.label: Autoscaling signal selection
nodes.summary: Autoscaling signal selection chooses metrics that indicate real demand, such as CPU, memory, queue depth, request concurrency, or custom service latency. Bad signals can scale too late, too far, or in the wrong direction.

nodes.label: Service mesh trade-offs
nodes.summary: Service meshes add traffic policy, mTLS, retries, telemetry, and routing at the sidecar or proxy layer. They also add operational complexity, resource cost, and debugging paths that teams must be ready to own.

nodes.label: Serverless operational constraints
nodes.summary: Serverless platforms remove server management but introduce limits around cold starts, execution duration, concurrency, packaging, network access, and observability. The runtime shape must fit the workload.

nodes.label: Secrets management and rotation
nodes.summary: Secrets management controls how credentials are created, stored, injected, rotated, audited, and revoked. Rotation must be designed so old and new credentials can overlap safely.

nodes.label: IAM least privilege
nodes.summary: IAM least privilege grants only the actions and resources needed for a role. It requires scoping by identity, environment, action, resource, condition, and operational break-glass paths.

nodes.label: Supply chain provenance
nodes.summary: Supply chain provenance records where artifacts came from, how they were built, and what source revision produced them. It supports auditability, tamper detection, and safer deployment policy.

nodes.label: Policy as code
nodes.summary: Policy as code evaluates infrastructure, deployment, or access rules automatically before changes land. It makes governance reviewable and testable instead of relying on manual memory.

nodes.label: Dependency update automation
nodes.summary: Dependency update automation opens reviewed, testable changes for package and action updates. It reduces stale dependency risk but needs grouping, rate limits, lockfile discipline, and CI confidence.

nodes.label: Observability baseline
nodes.summary: An observability baseline defines the minimum logs, metrics, traces, dashboards, and service metadata every production service should expose. It lets responders compare systems quickly during incidents.

nodes.label: Alert routing and ownership
nodes.summary: Alert routing and ownership connect symptoms to responsible teams, escalation policies, runbooks, and user impact. Alerts without owners become noise; owners without context burn out.

nodes.label: Incident command and postmortems
nodes.summary: Incident command coordinates roles, communication, mitigation, timeline, and follow-up during production incidents. Postmortems turn incidents into system improvements without blame.

nodes.label: SLO burn-rate alerting
nodes.summary: SLO burn-rate alerting pages when a service consumes its error budget too quickly across short and long windows. It connects alert urgency to user-visible reliability targets.

nodes.label: Runbooks and game days
nodes.summary: Runbooks document diagnosis and mitigation steps, while game days rehearse failures before real incidents. Together they turn operational knowledge into practiced team behavior.

nodes.label: Cost allocation and FinOps
nodes.summary: Cost allocation and FinOps connect platform spend to teams, products, environments, and unit economics. Good systems expose cost drivers early enough for engineering decisions to change them.

nodes.label: Internal developer platforms
nodes.summary: Internal developer platforms provide paved paths for teams to build, deploy, observe, and operate software. They should be treated as products with users, adoption metrics, support, and feedback loops.

nodes.label: Golden paths and service templates
nodes.summary: Golden paths and templates encode recommended architecture, CI, deployment, observability, security, and ownership defaults. They reduce repeated decisions without blocking teams that need justified exceptions.

nodes.label: Local development environments
nodes.summary: Local development environments should make common workflows fast and realistic without requiring production credentials. The design balances fidelity, startup time, dependency weight, and reproducibility.

nodes.label: Feature flag operations
nodes.summary: Feature flag operations manage targeting, ownership, cleanup, defaults, audit logs, and failure behavior. Without lifecycle discipline, flags become hidden production configuration debt.

nodes.label: Configuration management and dynamic rollout
nodes.summary: Configuration management separates deploy-time code from runtime policy. Dynamic rollout lets teams change behavior safely, but requires validation, auditability, scoping, rollback, and cache invalidation.

nodes.label: Platform API ergonomics
nodes.summary: Platform API ergonomics determine how easily product teams can use internal capabilities without learning every underlying system. Good APIs expose safe defaults, clear errors, stable contracts, and escape hatches.

nodes.label: IP addressing and routing fundamentals
nodes.note: Use this group to reason about address space, route selection, NAT, and global traffic paths before blaming application code.

nodes.label: DNS, TLS, and edge delivery
nodes.note: Use this group to connect names, certificates, proxies, CDNs, caches, and edge routing to real production reachability.

nodes.label: Transport protocols and performance
nodes.note: Use this group to explain latency, connection setup, packet loss, congestion, MTU behavior, and load-balancing effects.

nodes.label: Security and access control
nodes.note: Use this group to make network access explicit through firewalls, private links, zero-trust policy, and traffic protection.

nodes.label: Service networking and cloud topology
nodes.note: Use this group to design how services, VPCs, gateways, regions, discovery, and address families connect.

nodes.label: Observability and troubleshooting
nodes.note: Use this group to diagnose network behavior with captures, traces, probes, SLOs, and incident triage routines.

nodes.label: CIDR subnet planning
nodes.summary: CIDR subnet planning divides address space into ranges sized for hosts, growth, routing, and isolation. A good plan leaves room for expansion, avoids overlapping ranges, and keeps route tables understandable.

nodes.label: Private vs public addressing
nodes.summary: Private and public addressing define whether traffic can be routed on the public internet or must stay inside a private network boundary. Engineers should recognize RFC1918 ranges, loopback, link-local addresses, and the translation or proxy paths needed for egress.

nodes.label: Route tables and next hops
nodes.summary: Route tables choose the next hop for packets based on destination prefixes. Longest-prefix matching, default routes, blackhole routes, and asymmetric paths are core ideas for debugging reachability.

nodes.label: NAT and egress design
nodes.summary: NAT and egress design let private workloads initiate outbound traffic through shared public addresses. Designs must account for port exhaustion, source identity, logging, allowlists, and failure domains.

nodes.label: Anycast and global routing
nodes.summary: Anycast advertises the same address from multiple locations so routing sends users to a nearby or preferred site. It improves global latency and resilience but requires careful health signaling and traffic-drain behavior.

nodes.label: DNS record types and TTLs
nodes.summary: DNS record types and TTLs control how names resolve and how quickly changes propagate. Practical fluency includes A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, CAA, apex constraints, and cache duration trade-offs.

nodes.label: Recursive vs authoritative DNS
nodes.summary: Recursive resolvers answer client queries by consulting authoritative DNS servers and caching results. Knowing the difference helps diagnose stale answers, delegation mistakes, split-horizon DNS, and resolver-specific failures.

nodes.label: TLS certificate chain validation
nodes.summary: TLS certificate chain validation proves that a presented certificate chains to a trusted root and matches the requested host. Failures can come from expired certs, missing intermediates, name mismatch, weak policy, or incorrect time.

nodes.label: CDN caching and edge routing
nodes.summary: CDN caching and edge routing move responses closer to users while respecting cache keys, freshness, purge behavior, origin shielding, and request routing policy. The edge becomes part of the production system, not just a static asset layer.

nodes.label: HTTP proxy and reverse proxy behavior
nodes.summary: HTTP proxies and reverse proxies terminate, forward, rewrite, buffer, retry, and observe traffic between clients and services. Headers such as Host, X-Forwarded-For, and Forwarded become trust boundaries.

nodes.label: TCP handshake and connection lifecycle
nodes.summary: The TCP handshake and connection lifecycle establish reliable ordered byte streams, then tear them down with FIN or RST behavior. Connection setup, reuse, idle timeouts, and keepalives affect latency and failure handling.

nodes.label: TCP congestion and packet loss
nodes.summary: TCP congestion control adjusts sending rate based on acknowledgements, loss, delay, and congestion window behavior. Packet loss and retransmits can turn a healthy service into a slow one before application metrics show errors.

nodes.label: UDP, QUIC, and connection migration
nodes.summary: UDP gives applications datagrams without TCP's built-in reliability, while QUIC builds encrypted streams, loss recovery, and connection migration over UDP. This changes how latency, packet loss, and client network changes are handled.

nodes.label: MTU, fragmentation, and PMTUD
nodes.summary: MTU limits the largest packet a path can carry without fragmentation. Path MTU discovery failures can produce confusing partial outages where small requests work and larger responses stall.

nodes.label: Load balancer algorithms
nodes.summary: Load balancer algorithms choose targets with policies such as round robin, least connections, weighted routing, hashing, locality, or latency. The choice affects fairness, cache locality, stickiness, failure recovery, and hot spots.

nodes.label: Firewall rule ordering
nodes.summary: Firewall rule ordering determines which allow or deny rule applies first. Specificity, default deny, explicit egress, logging, and rule shadowing are essential for both security and debugging.

nodes.label: Security groups vs network ACLs
nodes.summary: Security groups and network ACLs apply network policy at different scopes and with different state behavior. Engineers should understand instance, subnet, stateful, stateless, inbound, and outbound rule implications.

nodes.label: VPN and private connectivity
nodes.summary: VPN and private connectivity link users, offices, clouds, and partners without exposing services publicly. Designs must cover routing, authentication, split tunnel behavior, overlapping CIDRs, failover, and auditability.

nodes.label: Zero trust network access
nodes.summary: Zero trust network access grants service access based on identity, device posture, context, and policy rather than broad network location. It shrinks implicit trust but requires strong identity, logging, and exception handling.

nodes.label: DDoS protection and traffic scrubbing
nodes.summary: DDoS protection and traffic scrubbing absorb or filter malicious floods before they exhaust application, network, or origin capacity. Useful defenses combine edge capacity, rate limits, challenge flows, filtering, and runbooks.

nodes.label: VPC peering and transit gateways
nodes.summary: VPC peering and transit gateways connect private networks with different scaling and routing properties. Topology choices affect blast radius, route propagation, inspection points, and ownership boundaries.

nodes.label: Service discovery and DNS-based routing
nodes.summary: Service discovery lets callers find healthy service instances or stable service names. DNS-based discovery is simple and portable, but TTLs, negative caching, health checks, and client caching shape failover behavior.

nodes.label: Ingress and egress gateway design
nodes.summary: Ingress and egress gateways centralize traffic entry and exit for policy, observability, routing, and security controls. They also become critical-path infrastructure with capacity and failure-mode obligations.

nodes.label: Multi-region failover routing
nodes.summary: Multi-region failover routing directs users away from unhealthy regions while balancing recovery time, data consistency, DNS or edge cache behavior, and traffic-drain safety. It must be tested before an incident.

nodes.label: IPv4 vs IPv6 dual-stack
nodes.summary: IPv4 and IPv6 dual-stack systems support both address families across DNS, routing, firewalls, load balancers, clients, and observability. Partial dual-stack rollouts can produce asymmetric reachability failures.

nodes.label: Packet capture fundamentals
nodes.summary: Packet capture fundamentals help engineers inspect actual traffic rather than inferred application behavior. Good captures choose the right interface, filters, time window, and privacy boundaries.

nodes.label: Traceroute and path diagnosis
nodes.summary: Traceroute and path diagnosis reveal likely network hops, latency jumps, and routing asymmetry. Results require interpretation because rate limits, firewalls, tunnels, and ICMP policy can hide or distort hops.

nodes.label: Synthetic network probes
nodes.summary: Synthetic network probes continuously test reachability, DNS, TLS, latency, packet loss, and regional routing from controlled vantage points. They catch network-path problems before users or services report them.

nodes.label: SLOs for network reliability
nodes.summary: Network reliability SLOs define measurable expectations for availability, latency, loss, DNS success, TLS success, and regional reachability. They connect lower-level signals to user-visible service behavior.

nodes.label: Incident triage for network partitions
nodes.summary: Network partition triage separates application failure from reachability, DNS, routing, firewall, load balancer, or provider issues. Responders need a disciplined path from symptom to packet path to ownership.
